for free after N1 3×5. Once the rook is gone the same 3-move skeleton
above is forced and it finishes in five half-moves. The longer 7-ply /
9-ply continuations rely on Black being allowed to give up the 4 square
and to shuffle the knight 6–4–6 indefinitely, but the knight shuffle
itself uncovers K2 to R1 on the first tempo, so the shuffle is not a
legal stall under the king-safety rule.

In ply counting that is a mate in 5, i.e. mate on White’s 3rd move, the
shortest forced line that is compatible with best defence. The 7-ply
presentation is the same idea with an extra king walk inserted, it is
not a distinct forced defence.

5.text:
On the 8 point strip let $m(i)=7-i$.  In the start

* $0\,K_{1}\;1\,N_{1}\;2\,R_{1}\;3\;\;4\;\;5\,R_{2}\;6\,N_{2}\;7\,K_{2}$

is $m$–invariant and

$K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}$ is  $N_{1}\!-\!R_{1}$ screened and
$K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}$ is  $N_{2}\!-\!R_{2}$ screened.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  Hence on an $m$–invariant position a
legal White move $p:i\to j$ can always be met by the mirror move
$p':m(i)\to m(j)$.  $p'$ is legal and restores $m$–invariance, and in
particular

$R_{1}$ checks $K_{2}$  $\iff$  $R_{2}$ checks $K_{1}$ .

A White move which leaves $K_{1}$ safe by the King–Safety rule can
never give a rook check on $K_{2}$ on an $m$–invariant position.
In particular

1. $N_{1}\;1\to3$     $1\ldots N_{2}\;6\to4$

is $m$–invariant and

$K_{1}\;0\;R_{1}\;2\;N_{1}\;3\qquad N_{2}\;4\;R_{2}\;5\;K_{2}\;7$

is again $m$–invariant.  As long as White stays inside the symmetric
class Black can always answer $p$ by $m(p)$ and the position can be
kept $m$–invariant for ever.  On an $m$–invariant position a rook
check on $K_{2}$ is the mirror image of a rook check on $K_{1}$ and
would be forbidden by King–Safety for the moving side.  Hence no
rook check, and a fortiori no check-mate, can ever be forced against
the mirror defence.  The unique immediate termination of the
symmetric class is the stalemate

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

after which Black has no legal move which keeps $K_{2}$ safe from
$R_{1}5$.  In the theoretical sense the position is a draw and White
has no forced check-mate at all.

*Remark.*  If Black abandons the mirror the usual textbook
exhibition is

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$    $R_{2}5\!-\!4$
2. $K_{1}0\!-\!1$
3. $N_{1}3\times R_{2}5$      $N_{2}6\!-\!4$
4. $R_{1}2\!-\!3$            $R_{2}4\!-\!3\times N_{1}$
5. $R_{1}3\times R_{2}3$     $N_{2}4\!-\!6$
6. $R_{1}3\!-\!4\times N_{2}$ $\#$ ,

i.e. the familiar $R_{1}4+$ mate, 3 White moves, 5 plies.  With the
most obstinate non-mirror defence $R_{2}5\to4$ the same idea can be
stretched to the conventionally quoted longest forced exhibition

1. $N_{1}1\to3$    $R_{2}5\to4$
2. $K_{1}0\to1$    $R_{2}4\to5$
3. $N_{1}3\times R_{2}5$    $N_{2}6\to4$
4. $R_{1}2\to3$    $N_{2}4\to6$
5. $R_{1}3\to4$    $N_{2}6\to4$
6. $R_{1}4\to6\#$ ,

the mate being delivered on White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move of
the game, the 7-ply 4-move version $1.N_{1}1-3\;2.R_{2}5\times N_{1}3\;
3.R_{1}2\times R_{2}3\;4.R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ being the shortest
forced mate that is usually quoted.  This is the longest forced
exhibition that is normally given once the mirror is abandoned.
∎

11.text:
On the 0-7 line the only checking device is a rook and the only
king-safety condition is

K1 not on the same open rank as R2 ,  K2 not on the same open rank as R1 .

Put $m(i)=7-i$.  In the start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the position is $m$–invariant.  Let $P$ be $m$–invariant.  If
$W:p\to q$ is legal for White then $q$ is empty or contains a Black
piece and the White king is still screened from R2 by the pieces which
remain on $0\!-\!5$.  Because $P$ is $m$–invariant $m(q)$ is empty or
contains a White piece and the Black king is screened from R1 by the
mirrored pieces.  Hence

$$B:m(p)\to m(q)$$

is a legal Black move and the position after $W\!B$ is again
$m$–invariant.  In particular a non capturing White move can always be
answered by the mirror and a checking rook move on $K2$ would be the
mirror image of a checking rook move on $K1$ and is therefore illegal
by King-Safety.  The mirror defence therefore keeps the game
$m$–invariant for ever as long as White never forces a capture which
removes the interposing piece which separates $R1$ from $K2$.

The first useful White move is

1. $N1\;1\to 3$

$K1$ is still screened by $R1\,2$ from $R2\,5$ and $K2$ is still
screened by $N2\,6$ from $R1\,2$.  Up to symmetry the only defence
which does not at once lose $R2$ is

1… $R2\;5\to 4$

The position is now
$0K1\;2R1\;3N1\;4R2\;6N2\;7K2$.  The mirror $N2\;6\to4$ is the
perpetual draw, the defence which keeps the game $m$–invariant.
The first player can break the symmetry only by forcing a capture on
the $2\!-\!7$ rank.  The fastest breaking line is

2. $K1\;0\to1$     $K1\,1$ is still screened from $R2\,4$ by $R1\,2$,
2… $R2\;4\times N1\;3$   forced, any $R2\;4\to5$ is met by $3.N1
3\times R2\,5$,
3. $R1\;2\times R2\;3$   $R2$ is gone, $K1$ is now permanently safe,
3… $N2\;6\to4$   forced, $N2\;6\to2$ would leave $K2$ on the $R1$
rank,
4. $R1\;3\times N2\;4\#$ 

After 4. $R1\,4$ the rank $4\!-\!7$ is $4R1\;5\;\;6\;\;7K2$ with both
$5$ and $6$ empty.  $K2\,7\to6$ stays on the $R1$ rank and is illegal by
King-Safety, $K2$ cannot capture $R1$ and there is no Black piece left
to interpose on $5$ or $6$.  $K2$ is in a normal rook check with no
legal move.  The mate is delivered on White’s fourth move, i.e. on the
7th half-move of the game

$1.N1\!1\!-\!3\; R2\!5\!-\!4\;2.K1\!0\!-\!1\;R2\!4\!\times\!N1\!3\;
3.R1\!2\!\times\!R2\!3\;N2\!6\!-\!4\;4.R1\!3\!\times\!N2\!4\#$ .

In the usual chess notation this is a mate in four moves of the side
to mate, seven plies in absolute terms.  In full round counting it is
four White turns, seven alternating turns $P1,P2,\dots $.
The same idea can be phrased as the textbook three-move king
capture

$1.N1\!1\!-\!3\;R2\!5\!\times\!N1\!3\;2.R1\!2\!\times\!R2\!3\;
N2\!6\!-\!4\;3.R1\!3\!\times\!N2\!4\#$ 

i.e. a mate on White’s third move, the 5th ply, if the capture of the
king $N1\;5\to7\times K2$ is admitted as a terminal win.  With the
strict $m$–invariant $N2\;6\to4$ defence the position can be kept
$m$–invariant for ever and the game is a theoretical draw; the 7-ply
rook mate above is the shortest forced termination once Black is
tempted off the mirror. ∎

9.text:
On the 0..7 strip the only checking piece is a rook and a rook check is
m i r r o r e d .  Put m(i)=7-i.  In the initial array

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the position is m-invariant and K1 is screened to R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is
screened to R1 by R2,N2.  After a White move p→q the position P′ satisfies

K1 is not on the R2 line in P′

iff

K2 is not on the R1 line in the position P″ obtained from P′ by the
mirror move m(p)→m(q).  Hence if P is m-invariant and p→q is a legal
White move the mirror move m(p)→m(q) is a legal Black move and P″ is
again m-invariant.  In particular a White move which would put K2 in
rook check would put K1 in rook check in the mirror image and would
therefore be illegal by the King-Safety rule.  So in an m-invariant
position a rook check can never be delivered.

Hence as long as Black answers a White move p→q by the mirror move
m(p)→m(q) the position stays m-invariant, neither king can ever be
put in rook check and the game can be kept symmetric for ever.  The
mirror defence is therefore a perpetual draw.  The only way to break
the m-symmetry is to capture a piece on its own mirror square, e.g.

1.R1 2×R2 5

0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

Now R2 has disappeared, N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1-5 and K2 7→6 is
blocked by N2, so Black has no legal move at all.  K2 is not in check,
the position is the stipulated stalemate draw and the termination can
be forced in two plies, one White move.

If Black is allowed to break the mirror, the familiar sacrifice is

1.N1 1→3  1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3  2…N2 6→4 forced
3.R1 3×N2 4+

R1 4 bears on K2 7 through 5-6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and is
illegal by King Safety, there is no interposition and no capture.
The check is delivered on White’s third move, i.e. on the 5th ply of
the game, the usual 3-move/5-ply mate.  With the most obstinate
non-mirroring defence the same idea can be delayed to the 9-ply line

1.R1 2→4 1…R2 5×R1 4
2.N1 1→3 2…N2 4→6
3.R1 4→5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 5→6#,

i.e. five White moves, nine half-moves, the conventional 5-move mate.
In particular with perfect mirror play White has no forced checkmate
at all; the best he can guarantee is the immediate stalemate draw
1.R1×R2, two plies, and the nominal mate is the 5-ply, 3-move-by-White
sacrifice quoted above. ∎

3.text:
On the 0--7 strip the only checking piece is a rook and a king can only be
kept safe by the two interposing pieces which are on the two rook lines

```
K1 0--1--2--3--4--5 R2          R1 2--3--4--5--6--7 K2 .
```

Hence after any legal move the moving player's own king has to stay
blocked from the opponent rook.  Up to symmetry the first legal first
move is

*1.N1 1--3*

K1 0 .1 R1 2 N1 3 .4 R2 5 N2 6 K2 7

and K1 is still screened by R1 2 from R2 5.  The only first move which
does not at once lose the R1 is this knight unblock.  After 1.N1 1--3
Black can at once lose the rook by 1...R2 5x3.  The essentially unique
shortest forced line is then

1.N1 1--3  1...R2 5x3
2.R1 2x3   2...N2 6--4 forced
3.R1 3x4#

The position after 2...N2 6--4 is

K1 0 R1 3 N2 4 K2 7

and R1 4 bears on K2 7 through the now empty squares 5 and 6.
K2 7--6 would still leave K2 on the R1 line and is illegal by the
King-Safety rule, R1 cannot be taken and no interposition is possible.
The black king is therefore in a normal rook check with no legal move.
The mate is delivered on White's third move, i.e. on the fifth
half-move of the game

1.N1--3 2.R2xN1 3.R1xR2 4.N2--4 5.R1xN2#

which is the conventional mate in three moves of the first player,
five plies in absolute notation.  With the usual 2...R2 5--4 defence the
same idea is transposed to the familiar seven-ply line

1.N1 1--3 R2 5--4 2.K1 0--1 R2 4--5 3.N1 3x5 N2 6--4
4.R1 2--4xN2#

and with the most obstinate shuffling of the N2 4--6--4 and K2 7--6--7
the same rook sacrifice can be delayed to the 9th half-move, i.e. the
fifth move of White, the textbook maximal stalling transposition of the
R1 4# motif.  This is the 5-ply, three-move mate which is normally
quoted for the position; in round notation it is the third move of
Player 1, five half-moves in total. ∎

10.text:
Under the King-Safety rule the only way to get a check on K2 is to get
R1 on the same rank as K2 with the interval  R1…K2 empty and with R2
gone.  K1 is screened from R2 by R1,N1 and K2 is screened from R1 by
R2,N2 for the whole of the opening.

1. N1 1→3 is the only first move which keeps K1 screened and which
opens the 2–3–4 corridor.  After

     0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the only Black reply which does not lose R2 at once is the
interposition

1… N2 6→4

which blocks  R2 5→3×N1.  Now

2. K1 0→1
2… N2 4→6

is forced,  N2 4→6 being the only move which does not leave K2 on the
R1–K2 line, and the position is again

0 . 1 K1 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 .

3. N1 3→5×R2
The rook is now gone, K1 is permanently safe and the 5–7 file is open
up to N2.

3… N2 6→4
is the only stall which does not give R1 3→6# at once.  After the
capture

0 . 1 K1 2 R1 3 . 4 N2 5 N1 6 . 7 K2

any move of N2 uncovers 6 to R1 2–7, so N2 is in a static pin.

4. R1 2→3
the first advance of the rook which keeps K1 screened by N1–R1.

4… N2 4→6
the only legal return which keeps K2 off the R1 line.

5. N1 5→?  the pin is now  R1 3–7 blocked by N1 5 and N2 6.  The
rook can be closed in one square at a time,

5. R1 3→4
5… N2 6→4

is again forced, and

6. R1 4→6#
R1 6 bears on K2 7 with 5 empty.  K2 7→6 is illegal by the King-Safety
rule, K2 cannot capture on 6 and there is no Black man left to
interpose on 5 or 6.  The king is in rook check with no legal move.

In ply counting the check is delivered on the 9th half-move, i.e. on
White’s 5th move,

1.N1 1→3  1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1  2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3  4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4  5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#

the usual 5-move, 9-ply mate.  Up to the conventional “mate in n
moves’’ counting this is the mate on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of
the alternation P1,P2,… .  The 5-ply, 3-move line

1.N1 1→3  2.R2 5×N1 3  3.R1 2×R2 3  4.N2 6→4  5.R1 3×N2 4#

is the shortest forced mate; the 9-ply line above is the longest
forced delay compatible with perfect stalling by Black. ∎

4.text:
The only piece which can give a check is a rook and after a move the
moving king has to stay screened from the opponent rook.  Put

m(i)=7-i .

After

1. N1 1→3

Black can restore the central symmetry by

1… N2 6→4

K1 0   R1 2   N1 3       N2 4   R2 5   K2 7

is m-invariant.  In an m-invariant position a White non–capturing
move p→q is legal iff the mirror move m(p)→m(q) is legal for Black,
for

* the distance and the direction of the move are preserved by m,
* m(q) is empty because q is empty and the position is m-invariant,
* the White move leaves K1 safe from R2 iff the mirror move leaves K2
safe from R1.

Hence after 1…N2 6→4 Black can always answer a White non-capturing
move by its mirror image and the position stays m-invariant.  In an
m-invariant position a rook check on K2 is the mirror of a rook check
on K1, i.e. the White move which would give check on K2 would at the
same time uncover K1 to R2 and is therefore illegal by King Safety.
In particular a rook check can never be delivered at all on an
m-invariant line.  White can of course break the symmetry by a
capture, e.g.

1.R1×R2

0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

and Black is now rookless.  N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5 and is
illegal, K2 7→6 is impossible and Black has no legal move at all.
The position is the stipulated stalemate, i.e. the only immediate
forced termination of the game is a draw.  With the mirror defence
the game can be kept m-invariant for ever, so in the strict
minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all.  The position is
a theoretical draw.

Remark.  Against the natural non-mirror defence 2.R2×N1 the classical
sacrifice is

1.N1 1→3  1…R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3  2…N2 6→4 forced
3.R1 3×4#

R1 4 bears on K2 7 through 5–6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1-line and is
illegal, and Black has no interposition or capture.  That is mate on
White’s third move, the 5th ply of the game, the shortest mate that
can be exhibited.  The same idea is usually quoted as the 7-ply
four-move mate and, with the most obstinate 1…R2 5→4 / 2…R2 4→5
stalling, as the 9-ply five-move line

1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.R1 2→… 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3×R2 5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 3→4 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 4→6#

which is the longest forced mate line that is normally quoted in the
room.  Up to the usual chess convention that is the mate in three
moves of White, five half-moves, often quoted as the seven-ply
four-move mate and, with maximal stalling, the nine-ply five-move
line. ∎

1.text:
On the 0..7 strip the only checking piece is a rook. In the initial
m–symmetric position

*0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2*

K1–R2 is screened by N1,R1 and K2–R1 is screened by R2,N2.  After the
opening

1. N1 1→3

K1 is still screened by R1 2 and K2 is still screened by R2 5,N2 6.
The natural losing defence is the capture on the decoy

1…R2 5×N1 3

and now the rook net is forced.  Up to notation

2. R1 2×R2 3
3…N2 6→4 forced, 6→4 is the only knight move which does not leave
K2 on the R1 3–7 line,
4. R1 3×N2 4+

R1 4 now bears on K2 7 through the empty squares 5,6.  K2 7→6 stays
on the R1 line and is illegal by the King–Safety rule, R1 cannot be
taken and there is no interposition.  The black king is in rook check
with no legal move.  The check is delivered on White’s third move,
i.e. on the 5th ply of the alternation

1 N1 1-3  1…R2×N1  2 R1×R2  2…N2 6-4  3 R1×N2#,

the text-book mate in three moves of the first player, five
half-moves in absolute counting.  This is the shortest demonstrable
mate.

Remark.  With the mirror defence 1…N2 6↔4 the position can be kept
centrally m–symmetric and the ordinary rook check can never be
delivered without at the same time uncovering K1 to R2.  In particular
Black can avoid 1…R2×N1 and the game can be kept drawn indefinitely;
in the strict minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at all.
The 9-ply stalling line 1 N1 1-3 1…N2 6-4 2 R1 2-3 2…N2 4-6 3
N1 3-5×R2 … which is normally quoted as the maximal delay, is the
five-move-of-White, nine-ply version of the same idea. ∎

2.text:
On the 8 points the only check that can ever be given is a rook check and
after a move the king which has moved has to stay out of the line of the
opponent rook.  In the initial array

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the two sides are centrally symmetric.  The only first move which does
not at once throw the R1 away is

1. N1 1–3

K1 is still covered by R1 2 and K2 is still covered by N2 6.  The
maximal stalling reply is the mirror interposition

1… N2 6–4

```
0 K1 3 N1 2 R1 5 R2 4 N2 7 K2
```

Now the rook line R1–K2 is 2–3–4–5–6–7 and the rook line R2–K1 is
5–4–3–2–1–0.  The only way to get a rook on the K2 line without
exposing K1 is to get rid of R2.  The quickest way to do it is to take
the rook with the knight,

2. N1 3×R2 5

The rook is gone so K1 is permanently safe.  The only move which does
not lose the king at once is

2… K2 7–6

N2 4–2×R1 and N2 4–6 both lose at once by N1 5×K2.

3. R1 2×N2 4

is now forced.  After the capture the file 4–7 is

```
4 R1 5 N1 6 . 7 .
```

and the king on 6 is still covered by the knight on 5.  The only legal
king move is

3… K2 6–7 .

4. N1 5–3

unblocks the rook.  R1 4 now bears on K2 7 through the empty squares
5,6.  K2 7–6 would stay on the R1 line and is illegal by King Safety,
K2 cannot capture R1 and there is no interposing piece left.  The king
is in a normal rook checkmate.

In ordinary notation

1.N1 1-3 N2 6-4
2.N1 3xR2 5 K2 7-6
3.R1 2xN2 4 K2 6-7
4.N1 5-3#

i.e. three White moves after the opening, four White moves in all,
seven half-moves in absolute terms, the mate being delivered on the
7th ply, the 4th move of the first player.  Up to the usual chess
convention of counting only the moves of the mating side this is the
well known mate in four of White, the 5-ply 3-move line
1.N1 1-3 R2 5x3 2.R1 2x3 3.N2 6-4 4.R1 3x4# being the
text-book mate against the non-mirror 2…R2×N1 defence.  In
full-round counting the win is forced on White’s 4th move, the 7th
half-move of the game.  The immediate 1.R1×R2 is the unique
immediate stalemate draw. ∎

15.text:
On the 0..7 strip the only piece which can give a check is a rook and a
check can be given only when the interval rook - King is empty.
In the start position

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the two kings are absolutely pinned

* K1–R2 : N1 1 , R1 2
* K2–R1 : R2 5 , N2 6

so that a move which uncovers the interval K–R is illegal by the
king-safety rule.  Up to a capture the position is centrally
m-invariant
$m(i)=7-i$.  As soon as White makes a legal move $p\to q$ the mirrored
move $m(p)\to m(q)$ is legal for Black and restores the $m$-invariance.
In particular a rook check on $K2$ would be the mirror image of a rook
check on $K1$ and would leave $K1$ under attack by $R2$, so that under the
mirror defence White can never give a rook check at all.  The mirror can
be broken only by a capture of the mirrored piece.

The first move which does not at once stalemate the game is

* $1.\;N1\;1\to 3$

$K1$ is still screened by $R1\;2$ and $K2$ is still screened by $R2\;5$.
The only defence which does not lose the rook at once is

* $1\ldots R2\;5\to 4$

$0\;K1\;1\;\cdot\;2\;R1\;3\;N1\;4\;R2\;6\;N2\;7\;K2$.
Now $K1$ can be put on the first square

* $2.\;K1\;0\to 1$

and Black is in fact forced to keep the $R1\!-\!K2$ line closed.  The
two essentially different continuations are

* $2\ldots R2\;4\times N1\;3$ and
* $2\ldots R2\;4\to 5$,

the first of them being the well known $3$-move sacrifice

$1.N1 1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2 5\!\times\!N1 3\;
2.R1 2\!\times\!R2 3\;2\ldots N2 6\!\to\!4\;
3.R1 3\!\times\!N2 4\#$ 

$R1$ on $4$ bears on $K2$ on $7$ through the empty squares $5,6$.
$K2\,7\to6$ stays on the $R1$-line and is illegal by King Safety and
Black has no interposition or capture.  This is the familiar
$5$-ply, $3$-move White mate, i.e. the seventh half-move of the game.

If Black keeps the rook on the $4$-square the mirror can be kept a little
longer.  With perfect stalling the longest line that can be forced is
the $R2\,5\to4$ defence and the king-shuffle

$1.N1 1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2 5\!-\!4$
$2.K1 0\!-\!1\;2\ldots N2 6\!-\!4\times R2$ - the rook is now gone and
$K1$ is permanently safe - 
$3.N1 3\!-\!5\;3\ldots N2 4\!-\!6$
$4.R1 2\!-\!3\;4\ldots N2 6\!-\!4$
$5.R1 3\!-\!4\times N2\#$ 

i.e. the ordinary $R1\!-\!4$ rook mate with the $R2$ removed.  With the
extra king waste $K1\,1\!-\!0$ the shuttle can be made

$1.N1 1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2 5\!-\!4$
$2.K1 0\!-\!1\;2\ldots N2 6\!-\!4\times R2$
$3.K1 1\!-\!0\;3\ldots N2 4\!-\!6$
$4.N1 3\!-\!5\;4\ldots N2 6\!-\!4$
$5.R1 2\!-\!4\times N2\#$ 

which is five White moves, nine half-moves in total, the fifth White
move being the mating $R1\times N2$.  In the ordinary chess
‘mate-in-$n$’ notation this is the textbook mate-in-three, the
$7$-ply line above, and with the maximal king waste the forced mate is
reached on White’s fifth move, the ninth half-move of the play.  This
is normally quoted as a forced mate in five moves of White, i.e. nine
plies, five full rounds, of the game.  Discarding the inessential king
waste the essentially unique forced line is the $5$-ply $3$-move
White mate quoted above.

6.text:
On the strip the only checking piece is a rook and the only piece which can
keep a king off a rook line is the knight which sits in front of it.
Up to the capture which breaks the central symmetry the game is

* 1. N1 1→3

the only first move which does not at once lose the R1, and after

* 1… N2 6→4

the position

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

is centrally symmetric.  The symmetry is broken by removing the
black rook.

* 2. N1 3×R2 5

R2 is gone, K1 is permanently safe and the line R1–K2 is now
R1 2–3–4–5–6–7 with the only blockers N1 5 and N2 4.  Black is now
forced.

* 2… K2 7→6

N2 4→6 would allow N1 5×K2 7 at once and N2 4×R1 2 loses the
rook and the king on 5×7.  After 2…K2 6

* 3. R1 2×N2 4

is the only rook move which does not open K1.  Now

0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 N1 6 . 7 K2

R1 is on 4 and bears on K2 7 through 5–6.

* 3… K2 6→7

is the only king-safe move, 6→5 would put the king on the R1 line
and is illegal by King-Safety.

* 4. N1 5→3

opens the R1–K2 line.  After 4.N1 3 the line 4 R1–5–6–7 K2 is clear.
K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and is illegal by King-Safety, there is
no interposition and the rook cannot be captured.  K2 is in ordinary
rook checkmate.

In ply counting this is

1W 1B 2W 2B 3W 3B 4W

seven half-moves in all, the fourth move of the mating side.  In the
usual mates-in-n notation this is the classical mate in four of White,
the 7-ply, i.e. seventh-turn, forced win.  In particular the
text-book shortest line

1.N1 1–3 1…R2 5×N1 3 2.R1 2×R2 3 2…N2 6–4 3.R1 3×N2 4#

is the 5-ply, three-move, mate which is obtained as soon as Black
fails to mirror, and the 7-ply line above is the longest delay that
perfect play can force.  Up to the conventional counting of a move of
the mating side this is the 4-move, i.e. the 7-ply, forced mate.  The
5-ply 1.N1–3 2.R2×N1 3.R1×R2 4.N2–4 5.R1×N2# is the shortest
realisation of the idea.

public_text.7:
The rook is the only checking piece and the only way to get a rook check on K2 is to clear the 2-3-4-5-6 interval. The first useful White move is forced

1. N1 1→3

K1 stays covered by R1 on 2, K2 stays covered by N2 on 6, and the R2–K1 line is now screened by N1 on 3. Any other first move either exposes K1 to R2 or leaves R1 on 2 where it can be taken at once.

With 1.N1 1→3 the only move that does not lose the game immediately for Black is

2. R2 5×N1 3

2. R2 5→4 is the mirror try. It leaves R2 on 4 with N1 on 3 between R2 and R1, so after 3. K1 0→1 Black has the forced 3…R2 4×3 and the position is essentially the same as above but with one extra White shuffle. The shuffle K1 0→1 is never needed for the mate and Black can always force it back in one ply, so the 7-ply exposition is not forced; it is White being wasteful.

On the forced capture line:

2… R2 5×3
Board: K1 0 R1 2 R2 3 N2 6 K2 7

3. R1 2×3
R2 is gone. K1 is now permanently safe because the opponent rook no longer exists, so White can now advance the rook at will. Board: K1 0 R1 3 N2 6 K2 7

After 3. R1×R2 Black has only N2 and K2. N2 is pinned to K2 by R1 on 3. The only legal knight move that keeps K2 out of the R1 line is

4. N2 6→4

4. N2 6→2 uncovers K2 to R1 3-7 and is illegal. 4…K2 7→6 is illegal because 6 would stay on the R1 line 3-7. So 4…N2 4 is forced.

5. R1 3×4#
Board: K1 0 R1 4 K2 7

R1 on 4 bears on K2 on 7 through the empty squares 5,6. K2 7→6 would stay on the rook line 4-5-6 and is illegal by King Safety. K2 cannot capture R1, there is no piece left to interpose on 5 or 6, and Black has no other men. The king is in check with no legal move.

That is White’s third move, i.e. the fifth half-move of the alternation P1,P2,P1,P2,P1. The mate is forced against the only defence that does not at once lose a piece, and the extra king shuffle K1 0→1 and the N2 6↔4 shuttling used in the 7-ply and 9-ply lines are not forced. Once R2 is removed on move 3 K1 is permanently safe, so the rook can be delivered in two plies.

In usual move counting this is a mate in three moves by White, five plies in total. The 7-ply lines quoted by several colleagues are a longer, non-forced exposition that inserts the unnecessary K1 0→1 shuffle and the R2 5→4 delay; with optimal stalling Black simply takes on 3 on move 2 and the mate is reached on the 5th ply.
public_text.13:
The first move is forced to be the unblocking of the white rook.

1. N1 1→3

K1 is still covered by R1 2 from R2 5 and K2 is still covered by N2 6 from R1 2.  After 1 the rank R1–K2 is 2-3-4-5-6-7 with N1 now on 3 between R1 and the empty squares. The only way to stop an immediate N1 3→5 capture of R2 is to take the knight.

The best defence is the capture:

2. R2 5×N1 3

After 2 the R1–K2 line is blocked by R2 on 3 and K1 is still safe because R2 is now on 3 with R1 on 2 in between.  Up to symmetry there is now only one White continuation.

3. R1 2×R2 3

The black rook is gone.  The position is

0 K1 . . R1 . . N2 7 K2

and K1 can never be attacked by a rook again.  Black has only N2 and K2 left.

N2 6→4 is the only legal knight move, 6→8 is off board and 6→4 keeps K2 out of the line R1 3–7 for one more move.  Any other move leaves K2 in the open line of R1.

4. N2 6→4

Now the line 3–7 is 3 R1, 4 N2, 5 ., 6 ., 7 K2.  The knight is the only screen.

5. R1 3×N2 4

R1 now sits on 4 with 5 and 6 empty between it and K2 7.  K2 is in rook check.

* K2 7→6 is illegal by King Safety, the king would still be on the R1 line 4-5-6.
* K2 cannot capture R1, distance >1.
* No black piece remains to interpose on 5 or 6.

Hence Black has no legal move with his king in check.  This is the ordinary rook mate.

The mate is delivered on White’s third move, i.e. on the 5th half-move of the game. In ply counting that is 5 turns, 1.N1 1→3, 2.R2×N1, 3.R1×R2, 4.N2 6→4, 5.R1×N2#.

Lines that try to stretch the game to 7 plies, e.g. 1.R1 2→4, 2…R2 5→4, assume Black voluntarily avoids 2…R2×N1.  2…R2×N1 is the immediate best defence and it collapses the position to the 5-ply sacrifice above.  The 7-ply knight walk and the mirror symmetry arguments only survive if Black refrains from that capture, which is not best play. With optimal stalling the forced win is the 5-ply, three White move, mate.
public_text.12:
On the 8 point line put $m(i)=7-i$.  The start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and $K_{1}$ is screened from $R_{2}$ by $N_{1},R_{1}$
and $K_{2}$ is screened from $R_{1}$ by $R_{2},N_{2}$.  A check can
only be given by a rook and after a move the mover's own king has to
stay on a rook closed interval.  In an $m$–invariant position

$R_{1}$ is on the $K_{2}$ line  $\iff$  $R_{2}$ is on the $K_{1}$ line

and the two intervals are mirror images of one another.  Hence a
move $p\to q$ of White is legal iff the mirrored move
$m(p)\to m(q)$ of Black is legal, because King safety is $m$–invariant,
and the mirrored move restores $m$–invariance.  In particular after

* $1.\, N_{1}1\to3 \qquad 1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$

we have

```
K1 0  R1 2  N1 3       N2 4  R2 5  K2 7
```

$m$–invariant, $R_{1}2\ldots7$ is blocked by $N_{1}3,R_{2}5,N_{2}4$ and
$R_{2}5\ldots0$ is blocked by $R_{1}2,N_{1}3,N_{2}4$.  If White now plays
any legal $p\to q$ the move $m(p)\to m(q)$ is a legal Black move and
the position stays $m$–invariant and both kings stay rook–safe.

In an $m$–invariant position a rook check on $K_{2}$ is the mirror
image of a rook check on $K_{1}$.  Delivering a check on $K_{2}$ would
therefore leave $K_{1}$ in the open line of $R_{2}$, which is forbidden
by the King–Safety rule.  The mirror defence can therefore be kept
forever and the position can be kept centrally symmetric for an
unbounded number of plies.  With perfect play the game is a
theoretical draw; White can never force a rook check and hence can
never force a checkmate at all.

*Remark.*  The symmetry is broken as soon as Black abandons the
mirror.  The textbook sacrifice which is normally quoted is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$  $1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$   $2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4+$

$R_{1}$ on $4$ bears on $K_{2}7$ through $5-6$, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on
the $R_{1}$ line and is illegal and there is no interposition or
capture.  That is White's third move, the 5th ply of the game, the
ordinary $3$–move $5$–ply mate, $7$ plies against the natural
$1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$ defence and $9$ plies against the most obstinate
stalling.  The $1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$ immediate termination is the
well known $1$ White move $2$ ply stalemate draw.  With perfect mirror
defence none of those lines is ever forced. ∎
public_text.8:
On the 8 point line let  $m(i)=7-i$.  The initial array

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and

* $K1$ is screened from $R2$ by $N1,R1$,
* $K2$ is screened from $R1$ by $R2,N2$.

A White move $p\to q$ is legal iff after the move $K1$ is not on an
unblocked $R2$ line.  In a $m$–invariant position the $m$–image
$m(p)\to m(q)$ is a Black move and

* $p\to q$ is empty $\iff$ $m(p)\to m(q)$ is empty,
* $p\to q$ is a capture of a Black piece on $q$ $\iff$
  $m(p)\to m(q)$ is a capture of the White mirror of that piece on
  $m(q)$,

and the $R$–safety of $K1$ after $p\to q$ is exactly the
$R$–safety of $K2$ after $m(p)\to m(q)$.  Hence in a $m$–invariant
position a legal White move can always be met by the mirror move and
the position is restored to central symmetry.

In a $m$–invariant position a rook check on $K2$ by $R1$ is the
mirror image of a rook check on $K1$ by $R2$.  A White move which
delivers check to $K2$ would therefore leave $K1$ in check from $R2$,
which is forbidden by King Safety.  Hence no check can ever be
delivered in a $m$–invariant position.

The only White move which destroys the $m$–invariance is a
self-pair capture $q=m(p)$.  The only self-pair capture White has
at once is

$1. R1\,2\times R2\,5$

$0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2$

and after it Black has no legal move at all: $N2\,6\to4$ would uncover
$K2$ to $R1\,5$, $K2\,7\to6$ is blocked by $N2$ and would still leave
$K2$ on the $R1$ line, and $R2$ is gone.  That is the unique
immediate termination of the game and it is the stipulated
stalemate, i.e. a draw, on the 2nd ply.

Apart from the self-pair capture every legal White move $p\to q$
with $q\ne m(p)$ can be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position stays
$m$–invariant.  In particular

$1. N1\,1\to3\; 1\ldots N2\,6\to4$

restores symmetry and

```
K1 0   R1 2   N1 3       N2 4   R2 5   K2 7
```

is $m$–invariant.  From now on $p\to q$ can always be answered by
$m(p)\to m(q)$, the kings never become unblocked and no rook check
can ever be delivered.  The game can therefore be kept $m$–invariant
for ever.  With optimal defence Black can force a perpetual mirror
draw and White has no forced checkmate at all.

Remark.  If Black abandons the mirror, e.g. $1\ldots R2\,5\times N1\,3$,
the well-known shortest exhibited mate is

$1.N1\,1\to3\;2.R2\,5\times N1\,3\;3.R1\,2\times R2\,3\;3\ldots N2\,6\to4$
forced
$4.R1\,3\times N2\,4\#$ 

$0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2$

the check is delivered on White’s third move, the 5th ply of the game,
the textbook 7-ply/4-move presentation being the same idea.  It is
not forced against the mirror defence.  With perfect play the
position is a theoretical draw and no forced win exists for White.
public_text.14:
I keep coming back to the N1 1-3 opening and the way the king safety rule pins the rook lines.

After 1. N1 1–3

K1 0 – N1 3 – R1 2 screens K1 from R2 5, and R1 2 – N1 3 – R2 5 screens K2 from R1. 
The only first move that does not at once lose the R1 is that knight walk.  

Now Black has to stop the immediate N1 3–5 threat on R2. The only legal
defence that keeps K2 safe from R1 is to take on 3.

* 1… R2 5×3

The capture is legal: after the capture R2 sits on 3, R1 on 2 is still
in front of it, so K2 is still covered by R2 3 and N2 6. K1 is still
covered by R1 2.

* 2. R1 2×3

The black rook is gone. K1 is now permanently safe. The only remaining
screen to K2 is N2 6. Any other black move either moves the king into the
R1 line or uncovers K2 to R1. The only move that keeps K2 out of the R1
line for one more ply is

* 2… N2 6–4

N2 4 still interposes on the 3–7 line. N2 6–5 is off the board for a
knight, N2 6–8 is off the board, and N2 6–4 is the unique interposition
that does not leave K2 in the line of R1 3.

* 3. R1 3×4

R1 is now on 4. The file 4–5–6–7 is empty up to K2 7. K2 is in rook check.
K2 7–6 would stay on the R1 line 4–5–6 and is illegal by king safety.
K2 cannot capture R1, and there is no black piece left to interpose on
5 or 6. Black has no legal move with his king in check.

That is the ordinary rook mate delivered on White’s third move, the
5th ply of the game, 1.N1-3 2.R1×R2 3.R1×N2#.

The 1…R2 5–4 waiting move that is used to get a 7-ply line is not a
harmless stall. After 1…R2 5–4 White has 2.K1 0–1 and Black is now
essentially forced to take on 3 anyway, R2 4–5 simply gives up the rook
for free after N1 3×5. Once the rook is gone the same 3-move skeleton
above is forced and it finishes in five half-moves. The longer 7-ply /
9-ply continuations rely on Black being allowed to give up the 4 square
and to shuffle the knight 6–4–6 indefinitely, but the knight shuffle
itself uncovers K2 to R1 on the first tempo, so the shuffle is not a
legal stall under the king-safety rule.

In ply counting that is a mate in 5, i.e. mate on White’s 3rd move, the
shortest forced line that is compatible with best defence. The 7-ply
presentation is the same idea with an extra king walk inserted, it is
not a distinct forced defence.
public_text.5:
On the 8 point strip let $m(i)=7-i$.  In the start

* $0\,K_{1}\;1\,N_{1}\;2\,R_{1}\;3\;\;4\;\;5\,R_{2}\;6\,N_{2}\;7\,K_{2}$

is $m$–invariant and

$K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}$ is  $N_{1}\!-\!R_{1}$ screened and
$K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}$ is  $N_{2}\!-\!R_{2}$ screened.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  Hence on an $m$–invariant position a
legal White move $p:i\to j$ can always be met by the mirror move
$p':m(i)\to m(j)$.  $p'$ is legal and restores $m$–invariance, and in
particular

$R_{1}$ checks $K_{2}$  $\iff$  $R_{2}$ checks $K_{1}$ .

A White move which leaves $K_{1}$ safe by the King–Safety rule can
never give a rook check on $K_{2}$ on an $m$–invariant position.
In particular

1. $N_{1}\;1\to3$     $1\ldots N_{2}\;6\to4$

is $m$–invariant and

$K_{1}\;0\;R_{1}\;2\;N_{1}\;3\qquad N_{2}\;4\;R_{2}\;5\;K_{2}\;7$

is again $m$–invariant.  As long as White stays inside the symmetric
class Black can always answer $p$ by $m(p)$ and the position can be
kept $m$–invariant for ever.  On an $m$–invariant position a rook
check on $K_{2}$ is the mirror image of a rook check on $K_{1}$ and
would be forbidden by King–Safety for the moving side.  Hence no
rook check, and a fortiori no check-mate, can ever be forced against
the mirror defence.  The unique immediate termination of the
symmetric class is the stalemate

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

after which Black has no legal move which keeps $K_{2}$ safe from
$R_{1}5$.  In the theoretical sense the position is a draw and White
has no forced check-mate at all.

*Remark.*  If Black abandons the mirror the usual textbook
exhibition is

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$    $R_{2}5\!-\!4$
2. $K_{1}0\!-\!1$
3. $N_{1}3\times R_{2}5$      $N_{2}6\!-\!4$
4. $R_{1}2\!-\!3$            $R_{2}4\!-\!3\times N_{1}$
5. $R_{1}3\times R_{2}3$     $N_{2}4\!-\!6$
6. $R_{1}3\!-\!4\times N_{2}$ $\#$ ,

i.e. the familiar $R_{1}4+$ mate, 3 White moves, 5 plies.  With the
most obstinate non-mirror defence $R_{2}5\to4$ the same idea can be
stretched to the conventionally quoted longest forced exhibition

1. $N_{1}1\to3$    $R_{2}5\to4$
2. $K_{1}0\to1$    $R_{2}4\to5$
3. $N_{1}3\times R_{2}5$    $N_{2}6\to4$
4. $R_{1}2\to3$    $N_{2}4\to6$
5. $R_{1}3\to4$    $N_{2}6\to4$
6. $R_{1}4\to6\#$ ,

the mate being delivered on White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move of
the game, the 7-ply 4-move version $1.N_{1}1-3\;2.R_{2}5\times N_{1}3\;
3.R_{1}2\times R_{2}3\;4.R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ being the shortest
forced mate that is usually quoted.  This is the longest forced
exhibition that is normally given once the mirror is abandoned.
∎
public_text.11:
On the 0-7 line the only checking device is a rook and the only
king-safety condition is

K1 not on the same open rank as R2 ,  K2 not on the same open rank as R1 .

Put $m(i)=7-i$.  In the start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the position is $m$–invariant.  Let $P$ be $m$–invariant.  If
$W:p\to q$ is legal for White then $q$ is empty or contains a Black
piece and the White king is still screened from R2 by the pieces which
remain on $0\!-\!5$.  Because $P$ is $m$–invariant $m(q)$ is empty or
contains a White piece and the Black king is screened from R1 by the
mirrored pieces.  Hence

$$B:m(p)\to m(q)$$

is a legal Black move and the position after $W\!B$ is again
$m$–invariant.  In particular a non capturing White move can always be
answered by the mirror and a checking rook move on $K2$ would be the
mirror image of a checking rook move on $K1$ and is therefore illegal
by King-Safety.  The mirror defence therefore keeps the game
$m$–invariant for ever as long as White never forces a capture which
removes the interposing piece which separates $R1$ from $K2$.

The first useful White move is

1. $N1\;1\to 3$

$K1$ is still screened by $R1\,2$ from $R2\,5$ and $K2$ is still
screened by $N2\,6$ from $R1\,2$.  Up to symmetry the only defence
which does not at once lose $R2$ is

1… $R2\;5\to 4$

The position is now
$0K1\;2R1\;3N1\;4R2\;6N2\;7K2$.  The mirror $N2\;6\to4$ is the
perpetual draw, the defence which keeps the game $m$–invariant.
The first player can break the symmetry only by forcing a capture on
the $2\!-\!7$ rank.  The fastest breaking line is

2. $K1\;0\to1$     $K1\,1$ is still screened from $R2\,4$ by $R1\,2$,
2… $R2\;4\times N1\;3$   forced, any $R2\;4\to5$ is met by $3.N1
3\times R2\,5$,
3. $R1\;2\times R2\;3$   $R2$ is gone, $K1$ is now permanently safe,
3… $N2\;6\to4$   forced, $N2\;6\to2$ would leave $K2$ on the $R1$
rank,
4. $R1\;3\times N2\;4\#$ 

After 4. $R1\,4$ the rank $4\!-\!7$ is $4R1\;5\;\;6\;\;7K2$ with both
$5$ and $6$ empty.  $K2\,7\to6$ stays on the $R1$ rank and is illegal by
King-Safety, $K2$ cannot capture $R1$ and there is no Black piece left
to interpose on $5$ or $6$.  $K2$ is in a normal rook check with no
legal move.  The mate is delivered on White’s fourth move, i.e. on the
7th half-move of the game

$1.N1\!1\!-\!3\; R2\!5\!-\!4\;2.K1\!0\!-\!1\;R2\!4\!\times\!N1\!3\;
3.R1\!2\!\times\!R2\!3\;N2\!6\!-\!4\;4.R1\!3\!\times\!N2\!4\#$ .

In the usual chess notation this is a mate in four moves of the side
to mate, seven plies in absolute terms.  In full round counting it is
four White turns, seven alternating turns $P1,P2,\dots $.
The same idea can be phrased as the textbook three-move king
capture

$1.N1\!1\!-\!3\;R2\!5\!\times\!N1\!3\;2.R1\!2\!\times\!R2\!3\;
N2\!6\!-\!4\;3.R1\!3\!\times\!N2\!4\#$ 

i.e. a mate on White’s third move, the 5th ply, if the capture of the
king $N1\;5\to7\times K2$ is admitted as a terminal win.  With the
strict $m$–invariant $N2\;6\to4$ defence the position can be kept
$m$–invariant for ever and the game is a theoretical draw; the 7-ply
rook mate above is the shortest forced termination once Black is
tempted off the mirror. ∎
public_text.9:
On the 0..7 strip the only checking piece is a rook and a rook check is
m i r r o r e d .  Put m(i)=7-i.  In the initial array

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the position is m-invariant and K1 is screened to R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is
screened to R1 by R2,N2.  After a White move p→q the position P′ satisfies

K1 is not on the R2 line in P′

iff

K2 is not on the R1 line in the position P″ obtained from P′ by the
mirror move m(p)→m(q).  Hence if P is m-invariant and p→q is a legal
White move the mirror move m(p)→m(q) is a legal Black move and P″ is
again m-invariant.  In particular a White move which would put K2 in
rook check would put K1 in rook check in the mirror image and would
therefore be illegal by the King-Safety rule.  So in an m-invariant
position a rook check can never be delivered.

Hence as long as Black answers a White move p→q by the mirror move
m(p)→m(q) the position stays m-invariant, neither king can ever be
put in rook check and the game can be kept symmetric for ever.  The
mirror defence is therefore a perpetual draw.  The only way to break
the m-symmetry is to capture a piece on its own mirror square, e.g.

1.R1 2×R2 5

0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

Now R2 has disappeared, N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1-5 and K2 7→6 is
blocked by N2, so Black has no legal move at all.  K2 is not in check,
the position is the stipulated stalemate draw and the termination can
be forced in two plies, one White move.

If Black is allowed to break the mirror, the familiar sacrifice is

1.N1 1→3  1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3  2…N2 6→4 forced
3.R1 3×N2 4+

R1 4 bears on K2 7 through 5-6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and is
illegal by King Safety, there is no interposition and no capture.
The check is delivered on White’s third move, i.e. on the 5th ply of
the game, the usual 3-move/5-ply mate.  With the most obstinate
non-mirroring defence the same idea can be delayed to the 9-ply line

1.R1 2→4 1…R2 5×R1 4
2.N1 1→3 2…N2 4→6
3.R1 4→5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 5→6#,

i.e. five White moves, nine half-moves, the conventional 5-move mate.
In particular with perfect mirror play White has no forced checkmate
at all; the best he can guarantee is the immediate stalemate draw
1.R1×R2, two plies, and the nominal mate is the 5-ply, 3-move-by-White

On the 0--7 strip the only checking piece is a rook and a king can only be
kept safe by the two interposing pieces which are on the two rook lines

```
K1 0--1--2--3--4--5 R2          R1 2--3--4--5--6--7 K2 .
```

Hence after any legal move the moving player's own king has to stay
blocked from the opponent rook.  Up to symmetry the first legal first
move is

*1.N1 1--3*

K1 0 .1 R1 2 N1 3 .4 R2 5 N2 6 K2 7

and K1 is still screened by R1 2 from R2 5.  The only first move which
does not at once lose the R1 is this knight unblock.  After 1.N1 1--3
Black can at once lose the rook by 1...R2 5x3.  The essentially unique
shortest forced line is then

1.N1 1--3  1...R2 5x3
2.R1 2x3   2...N2 6--4 forced
3.R1 3x4#

The position after 2...N2 6--4 is

K1 0 R1 3 N2 4 K2 7

and R1 4 bears on K2 7 through the now empty squares 5 and 6.
K2 7--6 would still leave K2 on the R1 line and is illegal by the
King-Safety rule, R1 cannot be taken and no interposition is possible.
The black king is therefore in a normal rook check with no legal move.
The mate is delivered on White's third move, i.e. on the fifth
half-move of the game

1.N1--3 2.R2xN1 3.R1xR2 4.N2--4 5.R1xN2#

which is the conventional mate in three moves of the first player,
five plies in absolute notation.  With the usual 2...R2 5--4 defence the
same idea is transposed to the familiar seven-ply line

1.N1 1--3 R2 5--4 2.K1 0--1 R2 4--5 3.N1 3x5 N2 6--4
4.R1 2--4xN2#

and with the most obstinate shuffling of the N2 4--6--4 and K2 7--6--7
the same rook sacrifice can be delayed to the 9th half-move, i.e. the
fifth move of White, the textbook maximal stalling transposition of the
R1 4# motif.  This is the 5-ply, three-move mate which is normally
quoted for the position; in round notation it is the third move of
Player 1, five half-moves in total. ∎

Under the King-Safety rule the only way to get a check on K2 is to get
R1 on the same rank as K2 with the interval  R1…K2 empty and with R2
gone.  K1 is screened from R2 by R1,N1 and K2 is screened from R1 by
R2,N2 for the whole of the opening.

1. N1 1→3 is the only first move which keeps K1 screened and which
opens the 2–3–4 corridor.  After

     0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the only Black reply which does not lose R2 at once is the
interposition

1… N2 6→4

which blocks  R2 5→3×N1.  Now

2. K1 0→1
2… N2 4→6

is forced,  N2 4→6 being the only move which does not leave K2 on the
R1–K2 line, and the position is again

0 . 1 K1 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 .

3. N1 3→5×R2
The rook is now gone, K1 is permanently safe and the 5–7 file is open
up to N2.

3… N2 6→4
is the only stall which does not give R1 3→6# at once.  After the
capture

0 . 1 K1 2 R1 3 . 4 N2 5 N1 6 . 7 K2

any move of N2 uncovers 6 to R1 2–7, so N2 is in a static pin.

4. R1 2→3
the first advance of the rook which keeps K1 screened by N1–R1.

4… N2 4→6
the only legal return which keeps K2 off the R1 line.

5. N1 5→?  the pin is now  R1 3–7 blocked by N1 5 and N2 6.  The
rook can be closed in one square at a time,

5. R1 3→4
5… N2 6→4

is again forced, and

6. R1 4→6#
R1 6 bears on K2 7 with 5 empty.  K2 7→6 is illegal by the King-Safety
rule, K2 cannot capture on 6 and there is no Black man left to
interpose on 5 or 6.  The king is in rook check with no legal move.

In ply counting the check is delivered on the 9th half-move, i.e. on
White’s 5th move,

1.N1 1→3  1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1  2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3  4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4  5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#

the usual 5-move, 9-ply mate.  Up to the conventional “mate in n
moves’’ counting this is the mate on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of
the alternation P1,P2,… .  The 5-ply, 3-move line

1.N1 1→3  2.R2 5×N1 3  3.R1 2×R2 3  4.N2 6→4  5.R1 3×N2 4#

is the shortest forced mate; the 9-ply line above is the longest
forced delay compatible with perfect stalling by Black. ∎

The only piece which can give a check is a rook and after a move the
moving king has to stay screened from the opponent rook.  Put

m(i)=7-i .

After

1. N1 1→3

Black can restore the central symmetry by

1… N2 6→4

K1 0   R1 2   N1 3       N2 4   R2 5   K2 7

is m-invariant.  In an m-invariant position a White non–capturing
move p→q is legal iff the mirror move m(p)→m(q) is legal for Black,
for

* the distance and the direction of the move are preserved by m,
* m(q) is empty because q is empty and the position is m-invariant,
* the White move leaves K1 safe from R2 iff the mirror move leaves K2
safe from R1.

Hence after 1…N2 6→4 Black can always answer a White non-capturing
move by its mirror image and the position stays m-invariant.  In an
m-invariant position a rook check on K2 is the mirror of a rook check
on K1, i.e. the White move which would give check on K2 would at the
same time uncover K1 to R2 and is therefore illegal by King Safety.
In particular a rook check can never be delivered at all on an
m-invariant line.  White can of course break the symmetry by a
capture, e.g.

1.R1×R2

0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

and Black is now rookless.  N2 6→4 would uncover K2 to R1 5 and is
illegal, K2 7→6 is impossible and Black has no legal move at all.
The position is the stipulated stalemate, i.e. the only immediate
forced termination of the game is a draw.  With the mirror defence
the game can be kept m-invariant for ever, so in the strict
minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all.  The position is
a theoretical draw.

Remark.  Against the natural non-mirror defence 2.R2×N1 the classical
sacrifice is

1.N1 1→3  1…R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3  2…N2 6→4 forced
3.R1 3×4#

R1 4 bears on K2 7 through 5–6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1-line and is
illegal, and Black has no interposition or capture.  That is mate on
White’s third move, the 5th ply of the game, the shortest mate that
can be exhibited.  The same idea is usually quoted as the 7-ply
four-move mate and, with the most obstinate 1…R2 5→4 / 2…R2 4→5
stalling, as the 9-ply five-move line

1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.R1 2→… 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3×R2 5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 3→4 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 4→6#

which is the longest forced mate line that is normally quoted in the
room.  Up to the usual chess convention that is the mate in three
moves of White, five half-moves, often quoted as the seven-ply
four-move mate and, with maximal stalling, the nine-ply five-move
line. ∎

K1–R2 is screened by N1,R1 and K2–R1 is screened by R2,N2.  After the
opening

1. N1 1→3

K1 is still screened by R1 2 and K2 is still screened by R2 5,N2 6.
The natural losing defence is the capture on the decoy

1…R2 5×N1 3

and now the rook net is forced.  Up to notation

2. R1 2×R2 3
3…N2 6→4 forced, 6→4 is the only knight move which does not leave
K2 on the R1 3–7 line,
4. R1 3×N2 4+

R1 4 now bears on K2 7 through the empty squares 5,6.  K2 7→6 stays
on the R1 line and is illegal by the King–Safety rule, R1 cannot be

On the 8 points the only check that can ever be given is a rook check and
after a move the king which has moved has to stay out of the line of the
opponent rook.  In the initial array

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the two sides are centrally symmetric.  The only first move which does
not at once throw the R1 away is

1. N1 1–3

K1 is still covered by R1 2 and K2 is still covered by N2 6.  The
maximal stalling reply is the mirror interposition

1… N2 6–4

```
0 K1 3 N1 2 R1 5 R2 4 N2 7 K2
```

Now the rook line R1–K2 is 2–3–4–5–6–7 and the rook line R2–K1 is
5–4–3–2–1–0.  The only way to get a rook on the K2 line without
exposing K1 is to get rid of R2.  The quickest way to do it is to take
the rook with the knight,

2. N1 3×R2 5

The rook is gone so K1 is permanently safe.  The only move which does
not lose the king at once is

2… K2 7–6

N2 4–2×R1 and N2 4–6 both lose at once by N1 5×K2.

3. R1 2×N2 4

is now forced.  After the capture the file 4–7 is

```
4 R1 5 N1 6 . 7 .
```

and the king on 6 is still covered by the knight on 5.  The only legal
king move is

3… K2 6–7 .

4. N1 5–3

unblocks the rook.  R1 4 now bears on K2 7 through the empty squares
5,6.  K2 7–6 would stay on the R1 line and is illegal by King Safety,
K2 cannot capture R1 and there is no interposing piece left.  The king
is in a normal rook checkmate.

In ordinary notation

1.N1 1-3 N2 6-4
2.N1 3xR2 5 K2 7-6
3.R1 2xN2 4 K2 6-7
4.N1 5-3#

i.e. three White moves after the opening, four White moves in all,
seven half-moves in absolute terms, the mate being delivered on the
7th ply, the 4th move of the first player.  Up to the usual chess
convention of counting only the moves of the mating side this is the
well known mate in four of White, the 5-ply 3-move line
1.N1 1-3 R2 5x3 2.R1 2x3 3.N2 6-4 4.R1 3x4# being the
text-book mate against the non-mirror 2…R2×N1 defence.  In
full-round counting the win is forced on White’s 4th move, the 7th
half-move of the game.  The immediate 1.R1×R2 is the unique
immediate stalemate draw. ∎
public_text.15:
On the 0..7 strip the only piece which can give a check is a rook and a
check can be given only when the interval rook - King is empty.
In the start position

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the two kings are absolutely pinned

* K1–R2 : N1 1 , R1 2
* K2–R1 : R2 5 , N2 6

so that a move which uncovers the interval K–R is illegal by the
king-safety rule.  Up to a capture the position is centrally
m-invariant
$m(i)=7-i$.  As soon as White makes a legal move $p\to q$ the mirrored
move $m(p)\to m(q)$ is legal for Black and restores the $m$-invariance.
In particular a rook check on $K2$ would be the mirror image of a rook
check on $K1$ and would leave $K1$ under attack by $R2$, so that under the
mirror defence White can never give a rook check at all.  The mirror can
be broken only by a capture of the mirrored piece.

The first move which does not at once stalemate the game is

* $1.\;N1\;1\to 3$

$K1$ is still screened by $R1\;2$ and $K2$ is still screened by $R2\;5$.
The only defence which does not lose the rook at once is

* $1\ldots R2\;5\to 4$

$0\;K1\;1\;\cdot\;2\;R1\;3\;N1\;4\;R2\;6\;N2\;7\;K2$.
Now $K1$ can be put on the first square

* $2.\;K1\;0\to 1$

and Black is in fact forced to keep the $R1\!-\!K2$ line closed.  The
two essentially different continuations are

* $2\ldots R2\;4\times N1\;3$ and
* $2\ldots R2\;4\to 5$,

the first of them being the well known $3$-move sacrifice

$1.N1 1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2 5\!\times\!N1 3\;
2.R1 2\!\times\!R2 3\;2\ldots N2 6\!\to\!4\;
3.R1 3\!\times\!N2 4\#$ 

$R1$ on $4$ bears on $K2$ on $7$ through the empty squares $5,6$.
$K2\,7\to6$ stays on the $R1$-line and is illegal by King Safety and
Black has no interposition or capture.  This is the familiar
$5$-ply, $3$-move White mate, i.e. the seventh half-move of the game.

If Black keeps the rook on the $4$-square the mirror can be kept a little
longer.  With perfect stalling the longest line that can be forced is
the $R2\,5\to4$ defence and the king-shuffle

$1.N1 1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2 5\!-\!4$
$2.K1 0\!-\!1\;2\ldots N2 6\!-\!4\times R2$ - the rook is now gone and
$K1$ is permanently safe - 
$3.N1 3\!-\!5\;3\ldots N2 4\!-\!6$
$4.R1 2\!-\!3\;4\ldots N2 6\!-\!4$
$5.R1 3\!-\!4\times N2\#$ 

i.e. the ordinary $R1\!-\!4$ rook mate with the $R2$ removed.  With the
extra king waste $K1\,1\!-\!0$ the shuttle can be made

$1.N1 1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2 5\!-\!4$
$2.K1 0\!-\!1\;2\ldots N2 6\!-\!4\times R2$
$3.K1 1\!-\!0\;3\ldots N2 4\!-\!6$
$4.N1 3\!-\!5\;4\ldots N2 6\!-\!4$
$5.R1 2\!-\!4\times N2\#$ 

which is five White moves, nine half-moves in total, the fifth White
move being the mating $R1\times N2$.  In the ordinary chess
‘mate-in-$n$’ notation this is the textbook mate-in-three, the
$7$-ply line above, and with the maximal king waste the forced mate is
reached on White’s fifth move, the ninth half-move of the play.  This
is normally quoted as a forced mate in five moves of White, i.e. nine
plies, five full rounds, of the game.  Discarding the inessential king
waste the essentially unique forced line is the $5$-ply $3$-move
White mate quoted above.

On the strip the only checking piece is a rook and the only piece which can
keep a king off a rook line is the knight which sits in front of it.
Up to the capture which breaks the central symmetry the game is

* 1. N1 1→3

the only first move which does not at once lose the R1, and after

* 1… N2 6→4

the position

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

is centrally symmetric.  The symmetry is broken by removing the
black rook.

* 2. N1 3×R2 5

R2 is gone, K1 is permanently safe and the line R1–K2 is now
R1 2–3–4–5–6–7 with the only blockers N1 5 and N2 4.  Black is now
forced.

* 2… K2 7→6

N2 4→6 would allow N1 5×K2 7 at once and N2 4×R1 2 loses the
rook and the king on 5×7.  After 2…K2 6

* 3. R1 2×N2 4

is the only rook move which does not open K1.  Now

0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 N1 6 . 7 K2

R1 is on 4 and bears on K2 7 through 5–6.

* 3… K2 6→7

is the only king-safe move, 6→5 would put the king on the R1 line
and is illegal by King-Safety.

* 4. N1 5→3

opens the R1–K2 line.  After 4.N1 3 the line 4 R1–5–6–7 K2 is clear.

no interposition and the rook cannot be captured.  K2 is in ordinary
rook checkmate.

In ply counting this is

1W 1B 2W 2B 3W 3B 4W

seven half-moves in all, the fourth move of the mating side.  In the
usual mates-in-n notation this is the classical mate in four of White,
the 7-ply, i.e. seventh-turn, forced win.  In particular the
text-book shortest line

1.N1 1–3 1…R2 5×N1 3 2.R1 2×R2 3 2…N2 6–4 3.R1 3×N2 4#

is the 5-ply, three-move, mate which is obtained as soon as Black
fails to mirror, and the 7-ply line above is the longest delay that
perfect play can force.  Up to the conventional counting of a move of
the mating side this is the 4-move, i.e. the 7-ply, forced mate.  The

realisation of the idea.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The board is m-invariant under m(i)=7-i. K1 is screened from R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by R2,N2. After a legal White move p→q the mirrored move m(p)→m(q) is legal for Black and restores m-invariance because King-Safety is m-invariant. In an m-invariant position a rook check on K2 is the mirror of a rook check on K1, so a checking move by White would leave K1 in the open line of R2 and is forbidden by King-Safety. In particular after

1. N1 1→3  1… N2 6→4

the position K1 0 R1 2 N1 3 N2 4 R2 5 K2 7 is m-invariant and any non-capturing White move can be answered by its mirror, keeping the game m-invariant forever and preventing any rook check at all.

The only way to break symmetry is a capture on a self-mirror square. The immediate self-pair capture

1. R1 2×R2 5

gives 0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2 and Black has no legal move that keeps K2 safe from R1 5: N2 6→4 would uncover K2, K2 7→6 is blocked/illegal. That is the stipulated stalemate draw in 2 plies, one White move.

With optimal mirror defence the game is a theoretical draw; White has no forced checkmate. The discussion therefore splits between strict minimax and the exhibited mates once Black abandons the mirror.

If Black abandons the mirror the textbook sacrifice is

1. N1 1→3  1… R2 5×N1 3
2. R1 2×R2 3  2… N2 6→4 forced
3. R1 3×N2 4#

R1 on 4 bears on K2 7 through 5-6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and is illegal by King-Safety, no interposition/capture remains. This is mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply of the alternation, the shortest demonstrable mate, 3 White moves / 5 half-moves.

Against the non-mirroring waiting defence 1… R2 5→4 the same idea can be delayed. The commonly quoted longest stalling exhibition is

1. N1 1→3 1… N2 6→4
2. K1 0→1 2… N2 4→6
3. N1 3→5×R2 3… N2 6→4
4. R1 2→3 4… N2 4→6
5. R1 3→4 5… N2 6→4
6. R1 4→6#

mate delivered on White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move. A 7-ply / 4-move version 1.N1 1→3 R2 5→4 2.K1 0→1 R2 4→5 3.N1 3×R2 5 … 4.R1 2→4×N2# is also quoted as the natural 4-move mate.

Unresolved/remaining: definition of “turn’’ – ply vs full round – and whether the problem intends the strict minimax result “no forced win / draw” via perfect mirror defence, or the conventional exhibited mate length once Black is presumed to break symmetry. The consensus in the current round is mirror = draw, shortest forced mate once symmetry is broken = 5 ply, longest forced exhibition with stalling = 9 ply, 5 White moves.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The initial m(i)=7-i symmetry is central. Start 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 is m-invariant and K1 is screened from R2 by N1,R1 and K2 is screened from R1 by R2,N2. Hence with the mirror defence
1. N1 1→3 1… N2 6→4
the position stays m-invariant and after any legal White p→q Black can play m(p)→m(q). No rook check can ever be delivered on an m-invariant line. The only way to break symmetry is a self-pair capture q=m(p). The only immediate self-pair capture White has is R1 2×R2 5, after which

0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

Black has no legal move that keeps K2 safe from R1 5: N2 6→4 uncovers K2, K2 7→6 is blocked by N2 and would stay on the R1 line, R2 is gone. That is the immediate 2-ply stalemate draw, the unique immediate termination.

Apart from that, every non self-pair White move can be met by the mirror and the game can be kept m-invariant forever. With perfect play Black can force a perpetual mirror draw, so White has no forced checkmate at all in the strict minimax sense.

If Black abandons the mirror the well-known sacrifice is the textbook line:
1. N1 1→3 1… R2 5×N1 3
2. R1 2×R2 3 2… N2 6→4 forced
3. R1 3×N2 4#
R1 on 4 bears on K2 7 through 5-6, K2 7→6 stays on the rook line and is illegal by King Safety, no interposition/capture. That is mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply. This is the shortest demonstrable mate.

1.N1 1→3 1… N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2… N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3… N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4… N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5… N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#
i.e. mate on White’s 5th move, 9th half-move. The 7-ply, 4-move White version 1.N1 1-3 R2 5-4 2.K1 0-1 R2 4-5 3.N1 3×R2 5 4.R1 2-3×... is the same motif.

The immediate stalemate after 1.R1×R2 is the only forced termination of the symmetric game. Unresolved is whether an infinite mirror play is considered a draw by repetition vs exhaustion, but the key point is the mirror prevents any forced checkmate.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The board is 0..7 with K1 0 N1 1 R1 2 . . R2 5 N2 6 K2 7. Only a rook can give check and King-Safety is “after your move your own king is not on an open rook line”. The two rook lines are screened initially by N1,R1 vs R2,N2.

The essentially unique first useful White move is 1. N1 1→3. K1 stays screened by R1 2 from R2 5 and K2 stays screened by N2 6 from R1 2. 1.R1 2×R2 5 is immediate stalemate for Black: after 1.R1×R2 Black has no legal move that keeps K2 safe from R1 5, N2 6→4 uncovers K2 and K2 7→6 is blocked/illegal. So White will not play it.

After 1.N1 1→3 the natural Black replies are
* 1… N2 6→4 – the mirror interposition,
* 1… R2 5→4,
* 1… R2 5×N1 3.

The capture 1… R2×N1 is the textbook losing defence. The forced line then is

1.N1 1→3 1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3
2…N2 6→4 forced – 6→2 uncovers K2 to R1 3
3.R1 3×N2 4#

R1 4 attacks K2 7 through 5-6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and is illegal by King-Safety, no interposition, no capture. Mate on White’s 3rd move, 5 plies total, 1 N1 1-3 2 R2×N1 3 R1×R2 4 N2 6-4 5 R1×N2#. This is the shortest demonstrable mate quoted by Colleagues 11,13,14,6 etc.

With the non-capturing defence 1…R2 5→4 the same idea can be delayed. A typical 7-ply exhibition is
1.N1 1→3 1…R2 5→4
2.K1 0→1 2…R2 4→5 or 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.N1 3×R2 5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 / 2→4 etc → R1 4# 
and with the most obstinate N2 6↔4 shuttle the conventional maximal delay is quoted as 9 plies, White’s 5th move:
1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#
i.e. mate on the 9th half-move, 5 White moves. Colleagues 10,14,15,2,6 give this 7-ply/9-ply rendering.

The mirror argument is the main counter-point. Put m(i)=7-i. The start is m-invariant and King-Safety is m-invariant. After 1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4 the position
K1 0 R1 2 N1 3 | N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
is m-invariant. In an m-invariant position a legal White non-capturing move p→q can always be met by Black m(p)→m(q) which is legal and restores m-invariance, because rook safety of K1 after the White move is equivalent to rook safety of K2 after the mirror move. The mirror defence therefore prevents a check from ever being delivered and the game can be kept m-invariant indefinitely. The only way to break symmetry is a self-pair capture, e.g. 1.R1 2×R2 5, which leads to the immediate stalemate draw described above. reflection_text.1:
The board is 0..7 with K1 0 N1 1 R1 2 . . R2 5 N2 6 K2 7. Only a rook can give check and King-Safety is “after your move your own king is not on an open rook line”. The two rook lines are screened initially by N1,R1 vs R2,N2.

The essentially unique first useful White move is 1. N1 1→3. K1 stays screened by R1 2 from R2 5 and K2 stays screened by N2 6 from R1 2. 1.R1 2×R2 5 is immediate stalemate for Black: after 1.R1×R2 Black has no legal move that keeps K2 safe from R1 5, N2 6→4 uncovers K2 and K2 7→6 is blocked/illegal. So White will not play it.

After 1.N1 1→3 the natural Black replies are
* 1… N2 6→4 – the mirror interposition,
* 1… R2 5→4,
* 1… R2 5×N1 3.

The capture 1… R2×N1 is the textbook losing defence. The forced line then is

1.N1 1→3 1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3
2…N2 6→4 forced – 6→2 uncovers K2 to R1 3
3.R1 3×N2 4#

R1 4 attacks K2 7 through 5-6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and is illegal by King-Safety, no interposition, no capture. Mate on White’s 3rd move, 5 plies total, 1 N1 1-3 2 R2×N1 3 R1×R2 4 N2 6-4 5 R1×N2#. This is the shortest demonstrable mate quoted by Colleagues 11,13,14,6 etc.

With the non-capturing defence 1…R2 5→4 the same idea can be delayed. A typical 7-ply exhibition is
1.N1 1→3 1…R2 5→4
2.K1 0→1 2…R2 4→5 or 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.N1 3×R2 5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 / 2→4 etc → R1 4# 
and with the most obstinate N2 6↔4 shuttle the conventional maximal delay is quoted as 9 plies, White’s 5th move:
1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#
i.e. mate on the 9th half-move, 5 White moves. Colleagues 10,14,15,2,6 give this 7-ply/9-ply rendering.

The mirror argument is the main counter-point. Put m(i)=7-i. The start is m-invariant and King-Safety is m-invariant. After 1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4 the position
K1 0 R1 2 N1 3 | N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
is m-invariant. In an m-invariant position a legal White non-capturing move p→q can always be met by Black m(p)→m(q) which is legal and restores m-invariance, because rook safety of K1 after the White move is equivalent to rook safety of K2 after the mirror move. Hence a rook check on K2 would be the mirror image of a rook check on K1 and would be illegal by King-Safety. The mirror defence therefore prevents a check from ever being delivered and the game can be kept m-invariant indefinitely. The only way to break symmetry is a self-pair capture, e.g. 1.R1 2×R2 5, which leads to the immediate stalemate draw described above. Colleagues 10,12,8,9,5,4 argue this is the correct minimax outcome: with perfect play White has no forced checkmate at all, the position is a theoretical draw, the best forced termination being the 1.R1×R2 stalemate in 2 plies.

Unresolved points: 
* whether the problem intends “force a win’’ in the strict minimax sense, in which case the mirror draw is the correct answer and there is no forced mate, or in the exhibition sense, in which case the 5-ply/3-move mate is the fastest and the maximal delay with non-mirror play is 7-ply/4-move or 9-ply/5-move depending on counting of king shuffles.
* counting of a “turn’’ – half-move ply vs full round. Most statements quote 3 White moves = 5 plies = 5 turns in half-move counting, and 4 White moves = 7 plies, 5 White moves = 9 plies.
* the role of capturing the king. The statement defines win by checkmate only, but several colleagues treat N1 5→7×K2 as a terminal win.

Current belief: the fastest exhibited mate is the 1 N1 1-3 R2×N1 2 R1×R2 3 R1×N2# line, 5 plies, White’s 3rd move. With optimal mirror defence Black can keep the position m-invariant forever, so strictly speaking White has no forced checkmate; the game is a draw, the immediate 1.R1×R2 stalemate being the shortest forced termination.

4.R1 3×N2 4#

and with maximal king / knight shuffling the same R1 4# motif can be

4.R1 2→3 N2 4→6 5.R1 3→4 N2 6→4 6.R1 4→6#.

mirror reply 1…N2 6→4 the capture 2.N1 3×R2 5 is met by the mirror

disappear and no rook check can ever be produced.  The mirror defence
can be kept forever and White has no forced checkmate at all in the
strict checkmate sense.  The best White can force against perfect
mirror play is the immediate stalemate draw 1.R1×R2.

The disagreement in the room is whether the mirror defence is
maintainable after a capture.  The capture 2.N1 3×R2 5 is mirrored by
2…N2 4×R1 2 which is legal: the final board has no R1, so K2 is
rook-safe, and knights do not give check.  Hence the symmetry is
preserved and the rook-check motif is never forced.  If capturing the
king with a knight is admitted as a terminal win the same capture
sequence gives a forced knight capture of K2 in three White moves,
i.e. five plies, the 5-ply/7-ply/9-ply exhibitions quoted above being
the longest delays obtainable once Black deviates from the mirror.

draw and no forced win exists. ∎

1.text:
The only piece that can ever give a check is a rook and the King-Safety
rule is $m$–invariant.  Put $m(i)=7-i$.  The start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and

* $K_{1}-R_{2}$ is blocked by $N_{1},R_{1}$,
* $K_{2}-R_{1}$ is blocked by $R_{2},N_{2}$.

Let $P$ be $m$–invariant.  If $W:p\to q$ is legal for White then $q$ is
empty or contains a Black piece and $K_{1}$ is still screened from $R_{2}$
in $P_{W}$.  Because $P$ is $m$–invariant $m(q)$ is empty or contains the
White mirror of the piece on $q$ and $K_{2}$ is screened from $R_{1}$ after

$$B:m(p)\to m(q)$$

so $B$ is legal and $P_{WB}$ is again $m$–invariant.  In particular a
non-capturing White move can always be answered by its mirror.

In an $m$–invariant position

$$R_{1}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{2}\iff R_{2}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{1}$$

and a White move which would put $K_{2}$ in a rook check would put $K_{1}$
in a rook check in the mirror image.  The move would therefore be
illegal by King-Safety.  No rook check, and a fortiori no checkmate,
can ever be delivered on an $m$–invariant line.

The first move which preserves King-Safety is

1. $N_{1}\ 1\to 3$

$K_{1}$ is still screened by $R_{1}2$ from $R_{2}5$ and $K_{2}$ is still
screened by $R_{2}5,N_{2}6$.  The mirror defence

1… $N_{2}\ 6\to4$

gives

```
K1 0  R1 2  N1 3       N2 4  R2 5  K2 7
```

which is $m$–invariant.  From now on every legal White $p\to q$ with
$q\ne m(p)$ can be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position stays
$m$–invariant forever.  The game can be kept centrally symmetric for
an unbounded number of plies and White can never force a rook check.

The only way to break the symmetry is a self-pair capture.  The unique
immediate self-pair capture is

1. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

```
0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2
```

$K_{2}$ is now on the open $R_{1}$ line.  $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover
$K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$ and is illegal by King-Safety, $K_{2}7\to6$ is
blocked by $N_{2}$ and would stay on the $R_{1}$ line, and $R_{2}$ is
gone.  Black has no legal move at all.  $K_{2}$ is not in check, the
position is the stipulated stalemate draw and the termination is
forced in 2 half-moves, 1 White move.

Hence in the strict minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at
all.  The position is a theoretical draw and the only forced
termination is the immediate $1.R_{1}\times R_{2}$ stalemate.

Remark on the exhibition line.  If Black voluntarily abandons the
mirror the textbook sacrifice is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$   1…$R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$   2…$N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ 

$R_{1}4$ bears on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$.  $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King-Safety, there is no interposition
and no capture.  That is mate on White’s third move, the 5th ply

1 N1 1-3 2 R2×N1 3 R1×R2 4 N2 6-4 5 R1×N2#

and the same idea is usually quoted as the 7-ply four-move and the
9-ply five-move stalling transpositions once the $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$
waiting move is inserted.  The 5-ply line is the shortest
demonstrable mate, but it is not forced against the $m$–mirror defence
described above. ∎

11.text:
Under the King Safety rule a legal move is the mirror image of a legal move.
Put $m(i)=7-i$.  The start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and

* $K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}$ is screened by $N_{1},R_{1}$,
* $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}$ is screened by $R_{2},N_{2}$.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  Hence on an $m$–invariant position a
legal White move $p\to q$ can always be met by

$$B:m(p)\to m(q)$$

and the position after $W B$ is again $m$–invariant.  In particular a
non-capturing White move can always be answered by its mirror and a
White capture can be answered by the mirror capture of the mirrored
White piece.

In an $m$–invariant position

$$R_{1}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{2}\iff R_{2}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{1}$$

so a White move which would give a rook check on $K_{2}$ would be the
mirror of a rook check on $K_{1}$ and would leave $K_{1}$ in the open
line of $R_{2}$, i.e. it would be illegal by King Safety.  After

1. $N_{1}\;1\to3\qquad1\ldots N_{2}\;6\to4$

```
K1 0  R1 2  N1 3       N2 4  R2 5  K2 7
```

is $m$–invariant.  Now every legal White $p\to q$ with $q\ne m(p)$ can
be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position stays $m$–invariant, the two
kings stay rook-screened and no rook check can ever be delivered.

Hence with the mirror defence the game can be kept centrally symmetric
for an unbounded number of plies.  In the strict minimax sense White
can never force a rook check and a fortiori can never force a
check-mate at all.  The unique immediate termination of the symmetric
class is the stalemate

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$,

two plies, and apart from that the position is a perpetual draw.

Remark.  If Black abandons the mirror the textbook exhibition is

1. $N_{1}1\to3\;1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3\;2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ ,

$R_{1}4$ bearing on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$, $K_{2}7\to6$ being illegal
by King Safety.  That is White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the
alternation, the shortest demonstrable mate, the $7$-ply $4$-move
version being the usual $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$ transposition and the
$9$-ply $5$-move version being the maximal stalling exhibition quoted
in the room.  None of those lines is forced against the $m$-mirror
defence. ∎
