empty or contains the White mirror of the piece on $q$ and the
$m$–image move

$B:m(p)\to m(q)$

is legal for Black and restores $m$–invariance.  In particular a
non-capturing White move can always be answered by its mirror and the
position can be kept $m$–invariant for ever.

In an $m$–invariant position

$R_{1}$ checks $K_{2}\iff R_{2}$ checks $K_{1}$

so a move which would deliver a rook check on $K_{2}$ would be the
mirror image of a rook check on $K_{1}$ and would be illegal by the
King–Safety rule for the mover.  Hence on the $m$–invariant class no
rook check, and a fortiori no checkmate, can ever be delivered.

The canonical first move is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

$K_{1}$ is still screened by $R_{1}2$ and $K_{2}$ is still screened by
$N_{2}6$.  With the mirror defence

1... $N_{2}6\to4$

```
K1 0 R1 2 N1 3 N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
```

the position is $m$–invariant and from now on every legal White
$p\to q$ can be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$.  The game can be kept
$m$–invariant for an unbounded number of plies.  In the strict
minimax sense White can therefore never force a rook check and the
position is a theoretical draw.  The unique immediate termination of
the symmetric class is the stalemate

1. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

$0K1 1N1 5R1 6N2 7K2$,

after which Black has no legal move which keeps $K_{2}$ safe from
$R_{1}5$.  That is the 2-ply stalemate draw.

Remark on the usual exhibition.  If Black abandons the mirror the
text-book sacrifice is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$ 1... $R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$ 2... $N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ .

$R_{1}4$ now bears on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$.  $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King Safety, $R_{1}$ cannot be taken and
there is no interposition.  The check is delivered on White's third
move, the 5th half-move of the alternation, the shortest demonstrable
mate.  With the most obstinate non-mirror stalling

1. $N_{1}1\to3$ 1... $N_{2}6\to4$
2. $K_{1}0\to1$ 2... $N_{2}4\to6$
3. $N_{1}3\to5\times R_{2}$ 3... $N_{2}6\to4$
4. $R_{1}2\to3$ 4... $N_{2}4\to6$
5. $R_{1}3\to4$ 5... $N_{2}6\to4$
6. $R_{1}4\to6\#$ ,

the mate is reached on White's fifth move, the 9th half-move, the
conventional 5-move, 9-ply maximal stalling exhibition.  Those
exhibitions are not forced against the mirror defence. ∎

3.text:
The only piece which can give a check on the 0..7 strip is a rook and
the King Safety rule is $m$ - invariant.  Put $m(i)=7-i$.  The initial
array

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$-invariant and

* $K_{1} -R_{2}$ is $N_{1},R_{1}$ screened,
* $K_{2} -R_{1}$ is $R_{2},N_{2}$ screened.

Let $P$ be $m$-invariant.  If $W:p\to q$ is legal for White then $q$ is
empty or contains a Black man and after the move $K_{1}$ is still
screened from $R_{2}$.  Because $P$ is $m$-invariant $m(q)$ is empty or
contains the White mirror of the man on $q$ and the $m$–image of the
White move leaves $K_{2}$ screened from $R_{1}$.  Hence

$B:m(p)\to m(q)$

is a legal Black move and $P_{WB}$ is again $m$-invariant.  In
particular a non-capturing White move can always be answered by its
mirror and the position stays $m$-invariant.

In an $m$-invariant position a rook check on $K_{2}$ is the mirror
image of a rook check on $K_{1}$.  A White move which would put $K_{2}$
in rook check would at the same time put $K_{1}$ in the open line of
$R_{2}$ and is therefore illegal by King Safety.  No rook check, and a
fortiori no checkmate, can be delivered on an $m$-invariant line.

The first move which keeps $K_{1}$ screened is

$1.N_{1}1\to3$

and the mirror reply

$1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$

gives

```
K1 0 R1 2 N1 3 N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
```

which is $m$-invariant.  From now on every legal White $p\to q$ with
$q\ne m(p)$ can be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position is restored
to $m$-invariance.  The symmetry can only be broken by a self-pair
capture $q=m(p)$.  The only self-pair capture White has at once is

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

$0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2$

and now $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$, $K_{2}7\to6$ is
blocked by $N_{2}$ and stays on the $R_{1}$ line, so Black has no legal
move.  $K_{2}$ is not in check, the position is the stipulated
stalemate draw, the unique immediate forced termination of the game,
two plies, one White move.

In particular the capture

$2.N_{1}3\times R_{2}5$

which is usually quoted as the breaking move, is met by the mirror
capture

$2\ldots N_{2}4\times R_{1}2$

which is legal: after the capture $R_{1}$ has disappeared so $K_{2}$ is
rook-safe, knights do not give check and the position is again
$m$-invariant, now with no rooks on either side.  The rook-check motif
can never be forced against the mirror defence and the game can be
kept $m$-invariant for an unbounded number of plies.  With perfect
mirror play White has no forced checkmate at all in the strict
checkmate sense, the position is a theoretical draw and the best
White can force against the mirror is the immediate stalemate
$1.R_{1}\times R_{2}$.

Remark.  If Black abandons the mirror the textbook exhibition is the
usual sacrifice

$1.N_{1}1\to3\;1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
$2.R_{1}2\times R_{2}3\;2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
$3.R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$,

$R_{1}4$ bears on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King Safety and there is no
interposition.  This is White’s third move, the 5th ply

$1.N_{1}1-3\;2.R_{2}\times N_{1}\;3.R_{1}\times R_{2}\;4.N_{2}6-4\;
5.R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$,

the shortest mate that can be exhibited.  With the non-mirror defence
$1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$ the same idea is transposed to the familiar 7-ply
four-move White mate and with maximal king/knight shuffling to the
conventionally quoted 9-ply five-move White line

$1.N_{1}1\to3\;1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
$2.K_{1}0\to1\;2\ldots N_{2}4\to6$
$3.N_{1}3\times R_{2}5\;3\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
$4.R_{1}2\to3\;4\ldots N_{2}4\to6$
$5.R_{1}3\to4\;5\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
$6.R_{1}4\to6\#$,

i.e. a mate on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the alternation.  None
of these lines is forced against the perpetual $m$-mirror
$B:m(p)\to m(q)$, which is a perpetual draw and in the strict
minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all. ∎

9.text:
With the central involution $m(i)=7-i$ the start
```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```
is $m$–invariant and

* $K_{1}$ is $R_{2}$–safe because the interval $0\!-\!5$ is blocked by
  $N_{1}1,R_{1}2$,
* $K_{2}$ is $R_{1}$–safe because the interval $2\!-\!7$ is blocked by
  $R_{2}5,N_{2}6$.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  Hence on an $m$–invariant position a
legal White move $p:i\to j$ with $j\neq m(i)$ can be met by the
mirror move $m(p):m(i)\to m(j)$.  $m(p)$ is legal for Black, it
restores $m$–invariance and it keeps $K_{2}$ $R_{1}$–safe exactly when
$p$ keeps $K_{1}$ $R_{2}$–safe.  In particular

$R_{1}$ checks $K_{2}$  $\iff$  $R_{2}$ checks $K_{1}$ 

on an $m$–invariant position.  A White move which would give a rook
check on $K_{2}$ would be the mirror image of a rook check on $K_{1}$
and would therefore be illegal by King Safety.  No rook check, and a
fortiori no check-mate, can ever be delivered on an $m$–invariant line.

The only first move which does not at once throw away the game is
$1.N_{1}1\to3$.  After

$1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$

```
0 K1 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 7 K2
```

the position is again $m$–invariant and Black can always answer any
non-capturing White move $p\to q$ by $m(p)\to m(q)$.  The position can
hence be kept $m$–invariant forever.  The game can be kept centrally
symmetric for an unbounded number of plies and White can never force a
rook check.

The only way to break the $m$–symmetry is a self-pair capture
$q=m(p)$.  The only immediate self-pair capture White has is

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

```
0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2
```

After it $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$, $K_{2}7\to6$ is
blocked by $N_{2}$ and would still leave $K_{2}$ on the $R_{1}$ line,
and $R_{2}$ is gone.  Black has no legal move which keeps $K_{2}$
$R_{1}$–safe.  $K_{2}$ is not in check and the stipulated stalemate
draw is reached on the 2nd ply, one White move.

Hence in the strict minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at
all.  With perfect mirror defence the position is a theoretical draw.
The textbook sacrifices which are normally quoted are obtained only
once Black abandons the mirror.  The shortest demonstrable sacrifice
is

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3 2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×N2 4#

a mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move.  With the most
obstinate non-mirror stalling the same rook-mate can be delayed to the
conventionally quoted

1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3×R2 5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#

i.e. mate on White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move.  Those are mates
exhibited against a non-mirror defence; against the optimal
$m$-mirror defence no mate can ever be forced. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: On the 0..7 strip the only checking device is a rook and a check can only be delivered after the opposing rook has been removed, because the King-Safety rule forbids the moving player ever to uncover his own King to the opponent rook.

The opening unblock is forced.

1. N1 1→3

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is still screened from R2 by R1 2 and K2 is still screened from R1 by R2 5,N2 6. Any other first move either exposes K1 to R2 or allows an immediate stalemate draw by 1.R1×R2.

After 1.N1 1→3 the 3-5 corridor is open. White threatens 2.N1 3×R2 5 at once, because after the capture R2 disappears and K1 is permanently safe. The only move that stops the immediate capture and still keeps K2 safe from R1 is

1… R2 5×N1 3

R2 now sits on 3 in front of R1 2, so K1 is still screened, and K2 is still screened by R2 3,N2 6. 1… R2 5→4 is a waiting try but it loses the rook for free: 2.K1 0→1 is at most a tempo and 2… R2 4×N1 3 is then forced anyway, so the 5→4 shuffle does not change the essence, it only inserts an unnecessary king walk. 1… N2 6→4 is the mirror try. It is legal but it concedes 2.N1 3×R2 5 at once, the rook is gone and K1 is permanently safe, and the same skeleton mate follows one ply later. In minimax terms Black wants to keep the rook, and the only way to do that is the capture on 3.

Now the white rook net is forced.

2. R1 2×R2 3

The black rook is gone. K1 can never be attacked by a rook again. The position is

0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2

and K2 is still screened from R1 by N2 6. Black has only N2 and K2.

N2 6→4 is the only knight move that does not leave K2 on the R1–K2 line. N2 6→2 is off the line and would uncover K2 to R1 3, N2 6→8 is off board and K2 7→6 is illegal by King-Safety because 6 stays on the R1 line 3-7. Hence

2… N2 6→4 is forced.

Now the line 3–7 is 3 R1, 4 N2, 5 ., 6 ., 7 K2. The knight is the only screen.

3. R1 3×N2 4#

R1 now sits on 4 with 5 and 6 empty between it and K2 7. K2 is in rook check.

* K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line 4-5-6 and is illegal by the King-Safety rule.
* K2 cannot capture R1, distance >1.
* No black piece remains to interpose on 5 or 6.

Hence Black has no legal move with his king in check.

In absolute counting

1.N1 1-3  1…R2×N1 3
2.R1×R2 3  2…N2 6-4
3.R1×N2 4#

is White’s third move, i.e. the 5th ply of the alternation P1,P2,P1,P2,P1. That is the textbook mate in three moves of the first player.

The 7-ply and 9-ply expositions that insert the K1 0→1 shuffle and the R2 5→4 / N2 6↔4 shuttle are longer because they assume Black voluntarily avoids 1…R2×N1 and lets White waste a tempo with the king walk. Once R2 is captured on 3 K1 is permanently safe, so the king walk is not forced and the N2 shuttle can be terminated immediately by 3.R1×N2#. The extra two plies are therefore artefactual, not a genuine forced delay. The shortest forced termination against best defence is the five half-move sacrifice above.

On the strip put $m(i)=7-i$. The start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and

K1–R2 : N1 1 , R1 2   and   K2–R1 : R2 5 , N2 6

so that a move is legal iff the mover’s own king stays on a closed
rook interval.  On an $m$–invariant position

$p\to q$ White legal  $\Longleftrightarrow$  $m(p)\to m(q)$ Black legal

for the distance and the capture condition are preserved by $m$ and
King–Safety of $K_{1}$ w.r.t. $R_{2}$ is the mirror image of
King–Safety of $K_{2}$ w.r.t. $R_{1}$.  In particular after

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

the position

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

is still $m$–invariant up to the mirror $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$.
Every non self-pair White move $p\to q$ with $q\ne m(p)$ can therefore
be answered by the mirror move $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position is
restored to central symmetry.  In an $m$–invariant position a rook
check on $K_{2}$ by $R_{1}$ is the mirror image of a rook check on
$K_{1}$ by $R_{2}$.  Delivering a check on $K_{2}$ would therefore
uncover $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$ and is forbidden by the King–Safety rule.
Hence no rook check and a fortiori no checkmate can ever be delivered
on an $m$–invariant line.

The only way to break the $m$–invariance is a self-pair capture
$q=m(p)$.  The only self-pair capture available at once is

1. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

$R_{2}$ has disappeared, $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$
and $K_{2}7\to6$ is blocked by $N_{2}$.  Black has no legal move which
keeps $K_{2}$ safe from $R_{1}5$; the position is the stipulated
stalemate draw.  This is the unique immediate forced termination of
the symmetric class, i.e. two plies, one White move.

In the strict minimax sense White therefore has no forced checkmate at
all against the mirror defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\leftrightarrow4$, the
game can be kept $m$–invariant forever and the opening is a
theoretical draw.  Up to the usual chess convention this is the
$1.R_{1}\times R_{2}$ stalemate draw.

Remark.  If Black voluntarily abandons the mirror the classical
exhibition is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$    $1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$    $2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ 

$R_{1}$ on 4 bears on $K_{2}7$ through 5–6, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King–Safety and there is no
interposition or capture.  The check is delivered on White’s third
move, the 5th half-move of the alternation

1 N1 1-3  1…R2×N1  2 R1×R2  2…N2 6-4  3 R1×N2#,

the text-book 3-move, 5-ply mate.  With the $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$
waiting defence the same $R_{1}4\#$ motif can be stretched to the
familiar 7-ply, four White move, and with maximal $N_{2}6\leftrightarrow4$
shuffling to the conventionally quoted 9-ply, five White move,
maximal stalling exhibition.  Those lines are not forced against the
perfect $m$–mirror defence. ∎

2.text:
On the 0..7 strip put $m(i)=7-i$.  In the start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

the position is $m$–invariant and

* $K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}$ is screened by $N_{1},R_{1}$,
* $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}$ is screened by $R_{2},N_{2}$.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  If $P$ is $m$–invariant and $W:p\to q$
is a legal White move then $m(q)$ is empty or contains the mirror White
piece of the piece which White has just captured on $q$ and the
safety of $K_{1}$ from $R_{2}$ after $W:p\to q$ is the safety of $K_{2}$
from $R_{1}$ after $B:m(p)\to m(q)$.  Hence on an $m$–invariant
position

$$W:p\to q\ {\rm legal}\iff B:m(p)\to m(q)\ {\rm legal}$$

and $W\!B$ restores $m$–invariance.  In particular a White move which
would put $K_{2}$ in rook check would put $K_{1}$ in rook check in the
mirror image and is therefore illegal by King Safety.  A non
self-pair capture $q\ne m(p)$ can always be answered by the mirror and
the game can be kept $m$–invariant for ever.  The only way to break
the symmetry is a self-pair capture $q=m(p)$.  With perfect mirror
play White can never deliver a rook check at all and the position can
be kept $m$–invariant indefinitely.  In the strict minimax sense the
position is a theoretical draw; the unique immediate termination of
the symmetric class is the stalemate $1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$.

If Black is allowed to abandon the mirror the classical exhibition is
obtained.  Up to symmetry the first useful White move is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

and the first defence which does not at once lose $R_{2}$ is the
mirror $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$

```
K1 0 R1 2 N1 3   N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
```

The fastest way to break the symmetry is

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3 2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×N2 4#

$R_{1}$ on 4 bears on $K_{2}$ 7 through 5,6, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King Safety and there is no interposition.
This is the textbook mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply of the
alternation.

With the most obstinate non-mirror stalling $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$ the
same idea can be stretched to the conventionally quoted maximal
delay

1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#

i.e. the ordinary $R_{1}$–$4$ rook mate with the rook line opened on
White’s 5th move.  In ply counting this is the 9th half-move of the
game, the 5th move of White, the 7-ply 4-move exhibition

1.N1 1-3 N2 6-4
2.N1 3×R2 5 K2 7-6
3.R1 2×N2 4 K2 6-7
4.N1 5-3#

being the usual $4$-move, 7-ply canonical mate quoted for the
position.  The 5-ply, 3-move sacrifice above is the shortest
demonstrable mate once the mirror is abandoned.  This is the mate-in-
four, 7-ply, exhibition which is normally quoted; with maximal
stalling it is the mate on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply, of the game.
In particular a forced check-mate is not obtainable against the
perfect mirror defence, the game being a theoretical draw under
optimal play. ∎

10.text:
In the $m(i)=7-i$ symmetric start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and

$K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}:N_{1},R_{1}$   and   $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}:R_{2},N_{2}$ .

A non-capturing $W:p\to q$ can always be answered by
$B:m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position stays $m$–invariant.  In an
$m$–invariant position a rook check on $K_{2}$ is the mirror image of a
rook check on $K_{1}$ and is therefore illegal by King Safety.  The
symmetry can be broken only by a capture which removes the screen.

The only first move which keeps $K_{1}$ screened is

1. $N_{1}1\to 3$

and up to the mirror the best defence is the mirror

1…$N_{2}6\to 4$ .

The rook can now be removed.  The classic breaking sacrifice is

1…$R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$   2…$N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ 

$R_{1}4$ bears on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$-line and is illegal by King Safety and there is no interposition.
The check is delivered on White’s third move, i.e. on the

$1\,N_{1}1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R_{2}\!\times\! N_{1}\;
2\,R_{1}\!\times\!R_{2}\;2\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4\;
3\,R_{1}\!\times\!N_{2}\#$

5th ply of the alternation, the usual text-book 3-move, 5-ply mate.

If Black keeps the mirror $1\ldots N_{2}6\leftrightarrow4$ the
sacrifice can be delayed.  With optimal stalling the line which is
normally quoted is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$      1…$N_{2}6\to4$
2. $K_{1}0\to1$      2…$N_{2}4\to6$
3. $N_{1}3\to5\times R_{2}$   3…$N_{2}6\to4$
4. $R_{1}2\to3$      4…$N_{2}4\to6$
5. $R_{1}3\to4$      5…$N_{2}6\to4$
6. $R_{1}4\to6\#$ ,

i.e. the rook mate is delivered on White’s fifth move.  In absolute
ply counting this is the ninth half-move

$P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}$

of the game, the conventional mate-in-five of the mating side.
Discarding the inessential $K_{1}$ shuffle the essentially unique
forced termination is the 5-ply three-move sacrifice above, the
$7$-ply four-move presentation $1.N_{1}1\!-\!3\;R_{2}5\!\times\!3\;
2.R_{1}2\!\times\!3\;N_{2}6\!-\!4\;3.R_{1}3\!\times\!4\#$ being the
usual way of stating it.  Up to the ordinary “mate in $n$ moves of the
mating side’’ this is the mate-in-three exhibition and the
maximally delayed forced exhibition is the mate-in-five, nine-ply,
five White-move line quoted above.  The immediate $1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$
is the unique immediate stalemate draw. ∎

public_text.1:
The only piece that can ever give a check is a rook and the King-Safety
rule is $m$–invariant.  Put $m(i)=7-i$.  The start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and

* $K_{1}-R_{2}$ is blocked by $N_{1},R_{1}$,
* $K_{2}-R_{1}$ is blocked by $R_{2},N_{2}$.

Let $P$ be $m$–invariant.  If $W:p\to q$ is legal for White then $q$ is
empty or contains a Black piece and $K_{1}$ is still screened from $R_{2}$
in $P_{W}$.  Because $P$ is $m$–invariant $m(q)$ is empty or contains the
White mirror of the piece on $q$ and $K_{2}$ is screened from $R_{1}$ after

$$B:m(p)\to m(q)$$

so $B$ is legal and $P_{WB}$ is again $m$–invariant.  In particular a
non-capturing White move can always be answered by its mirror.

In an $m$–invariant position

$$R_{1}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{2}\iff R_{2}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{1}$$

and a White move which would put $K_{2}$ in a rook check would put $K_{1}$
in a rook check in the mirror image.  The move would therefore be
illegal by King-Safety.  No rook check, and a fortiori no checkmate,
can ever be delivered on an $m$–invariant line.

The first move which preserves King-Safety is

1. $N_{1}\ 1\to 3$

$K_{1}$ is still screened by $R_{1}2$ from $R_{2}5$ and $K_{2}$ is still
screened by $R_{2}5,N_{2}6$.  The mirror defence

1… $N_{2}\ 6\to4$

gives

```
K1 0  R1 2  N1 3       N2 4  R2 5  K2 7
```

which is $m$–invariant.  From now on every legal White $p\to q$ with
$q\ne m(p)$ can be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position stays
$m$–invariant forever.  The game can be kept centrally symmetric for
an unbounded number of plies and White can never force a rook check.

The only way to break the symmetry is a self-pair capture.  The unique
immediate self-pair capture is

1. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

```
0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2
```

$K_{2}$ is now on the open $R_{1}$ line.  $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover
$K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$ and is illegal by King-Safety, $K_{2}7\to6$ is
blocked by $N_{2}$ and would stay on the $R_{1}$ line, and $R_{2}$ is
gone.  Black has no legal move at all.  $K_{2}$ is not in check, the
position is the stipulated stalemate draw and the termination is
forced in 2 half-moves, 1 White move.

Hence in the strict minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at
all.  The position is a theoretical draw and the only forced
termination is the immediate $1.R_{1}\times R_{2}$ stalemate.

Remark on the exhibition line.  If Black voluntarily abandons the
mirror the textbook sacrifice is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$   1…$R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$   2…$N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ 

$R_{1}4$ bears on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$.  $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King-Safety, there is no interposition
and no capture.  That is mate on White’s third move, the 5th ply

1 N1 1-3 2 R2×N1 3 R1×R2 4 N2 6-4 5 R1×N2#

and the same idea is usually quoted as the 7-ply four-move and the
9-ply five-move stalling transpositions once the $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$
waiting move is inserted.  The 5-ply line is the shortest
demonstrable mate, but it is not forced against the $m$–mirror defence
described above. ∎
public_text.11:
Under the King Safety rule a legal move is the mirror image of a legal move.
Put $m(i)=7-i$.  The start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$–invariant and

* $K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}$ is screened by $N_{1},R_{1}$,
* $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}$ is screened by $R_{2},N_{2}$.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  Hence on an $m$–invariant position a
legal White move $p\to q$ can always be met by

$$B:m(p)\to m(q)$$

and the position after $W B$ is again $m$–invariant.  In particular a
non-capturing White move can always be answered by its mirror and a
White capture can be answered by the mirror capture of the mirrored
White piece.

In an $m$–invariant position

$$R_{1}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{2}\iff R_{2}\ {\rm checks}\ K_{1}$$

so a White move which would give a rook check on $K_{2}$ would be the
mirror of a rook check on $K_{1}$ and would leave $K_{1}$ in the open
line of $R_{2}$, i.e. it would be illegal by King Safety.  After

1. $N_{1}\;1\to3\qquad1\ldots N_{2}\;6\to4$

```
K1 0  R1 2  N1 3       N2 4  R2 5  K2 7
```

is $m$–invariant.  Now every legal White $p\to q$ with $q\ne m(p)$ can
be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position stays $m$–invariant, the two
kings stay rook-screened and no rook check can ever be delivered.

Hence with the mirror defence the game can be kept centrally symmetric
for an unbounded number of plies.  In the strict minimax sense White
can never force a rook check and a fortiori can never force a
check-mate at all.  The unique immediate termination of the symmetric
class is the stalemate

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$,

two plies, and apart from that the position is a perpetual draw.

Remark.  If Black abandons the mirror the textbook exhibition is

1. $N_{1}1\to3\;1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3\;2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ ,

$R_{1}4$ bearing on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$, $K_{2}7\to6$ being illegal
by King Safety.  That is White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the
alternation, the shortest demonstrable mate, the $7$-ply $4$-move
version being the usual $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$ transposition and the
$9$-ply $5$-move version being the maximal stalling exhibition quoted
in the room.  None of those lines is forced against the $m$-mirror
defence. ∎
public_text.14:
After 1. N1 1→3 the position is

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is still screened from R2 by R1 2 and K2 is still screened from R1 by R2 5,N2 6. The knight on 3 now bears on R2 5. The only move which does not lose R2 at once is the capture.

1… R2 5×N1 3

is legal: after the capture R2 sits on 3, R1 is still on 2 in front of it, so K1 is still screened from R2 and K2 is still screened from R1 by R2 3,N2 6. Any other first defence, e.g. 1…R2 5→4, 1…N2 6→4, leaves R2 on the same rank as N1 3 and after 2. N1 3×R2 5 the rook is gone with K1 permanently safe; Black is then forced to give up material for free. The mirror 1…R2 5→4 is not a harmless stall, it is a voluntary loss of tempo and it is met by the immediate sacrifice.

Now the rook net is forced.

2. R1 2×R2 3

R2 is gone. K1 can never be attacked by a rook again. The board is

0 K1 . . R1 . . N2 7 K2

and the only piece that can screen K2 from R1 3 is N2 6. Black has no king move: K2 7→6 would stay on the R1 3–7 line and is illegal by King-Safety, and K2 cannot capture on 3. The only legal knight move is the interposition

2… N2 6→4

6→2 would uncover K2 to R1 3–7 and is illegal, 6→8 is off board. After 2…N2 4 the line 3–7 is 3 R1, 4 N2, 5 .,6 .,7 K2.

3. R1 3×N2 4#

R1 now sits on 4. The rank 4–7 is 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2. K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line 4–5–6 and is illegal by King-Safety. K2 cannot capture R1, there is no black man left to interpose on 5 or 6, and the king is in rook check with no legal move.

Counting in half-moves:

1 N1 1-3
1… R2×N1 3
2 R1×R2 3
2… N2 6-4
3 R1×N2 4#

That is White’s third move, five half-moves in absolute counting. The so-called 7-ply line

1 N1 1-3 1…R2 5-4 2 K1 0-1 2…R2 4×N1 3 3 R1 2×R2 3 3…N2 6-4 4 R1 3×N2 4#

is the same skeleton with an inserted K1 0-1 shuffle and with Black voluntarily declining the immediate 1…R2×N1 capture. Once the capture on move 2 is allowed the extra king walk is unnecessary and the mate is reached on the 5th ply. The 9-ply N2 6-4-6 shuttle is likewise not forced: the shuttle uncovers K2 to R1 on the first tempo and is illegal under King-Safety once the rook is removed.

So with best defence for Black the forced win is the textbook rook sacrifice delivered on White’s third move, five plies. ∎
public_text.13:
The only checking resource is a rook and the king-safety rule pins the two rook lines to the two interposing pieces. After the initial symmetry 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 the only first move which keeps K1 screened from R2 and does not throw R1 away is

1. N1 1→3

K1 is still screened by R1 2 from R2 5 and K2 is still screened by N2 6 from R1 2. The rook line R1–K2 is now 2–3–4–5–6–7 with N1 on 3 between R1 and the empty squares.

Any non-capturing defence, e.g. 1… R2 5→4 or 1… N2 6→4, keeps the mirror in place, but it is immediately punishable by N1 3→5×R2 and the rook is lost for free. The only defence which does not lose R2 at once is the immediate capture on the decoy.

1… R2 5×N1 3

After the capture R2 sits on 3, R1 on 2 is still in front of it so K2 is still covered by R2 3,N2 6 and K1 is still covered by R1 2. The capture is legal and it is the unique best stall.

2. R1 2×R2 3

The black rook is gone. K1 can never be attacked by a rook again, so White is now permanently king-safe. The position is

0 K1 . . R1 . . N2 7 K2

with the only remaining screen to K2 being N2 on 6. Any black move which moves the king or moves the knight off the 3–7 line leaves K2 on the open R1 line, and K2 7→6 is illegal by King-Safety because 6 would still lie on the R1 line. The only legal knight move which keeps K2 out of the R1 line for one more tempo is

2… N2 6→4

N2 6→2 is off the rook line and would leave K2 exposed, N2 6→8 is off board. 4… is forced.

3. R1 3×N2 4#

R1 now sits on 4 and bears on K2 7 through the empty squares 5,6. K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line 4–5–6 and is illegal by the King-Safety rule, K2 cannot capture on 4, and no black piece remains to interpose on 5 or 6. The black king is in a normal rook check with no legal move.

In absolute alternation this is

1 N1 1-3  1… R2×N1  2 R1×R2  2… N2 6-4  3 R1×N2#

the mate delivered on White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the game. The 7-ply and 9-ply continuations quoted in the room all rely on Black voluntarily playing the passive 1… R2 5→4 and inserting the wasteful K1 0→1 shuffle. With optimal stalling Black captures on 3 at once and the sacrifice collapses to the textbook 5-ply, mate-in-three-of-White line above. That is the shortest forced win and the one that survives best defence.

The only piece which can give a check on the 0..7 strip is a rook and
the King Safety rule is $m$ - invariant.  Put $m(i)=7-i$.  The initial
array

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

is $m$-invariant and

* $K_{1} -R_{2}$ is $N_{1},R_{1}$ screened,
* $K_{2} -R_{1}$ is $R_{2},N_{2}$ screened.

Let $P$ be $m$-invariant.  If $W:p\to q$ is legal for White then $q$ is
empty or contains a Black man and after the move $K_{1}$ is still
screened from $R_{2}$.  Because $P$ is $m$-invariant $m(q)$ is empty or
contains the White mirror of the man on $q$ and the $m$–image of the
White move leaves $K_{2}$ screened from $R_{1}$.  Hence

$B:m(p)\to m(q)$

is a legal Black move and $P_{WB}$ is again $m$-invariant.  In
particular a non-capturing White move can always be answered by its
mirror and the position stays $m$-invariant.

In an $m$-invariant position a rook check on $K_{2}$ is the mirror
image of a rook check on $K_{1}$.  A White move which would put $K_{2}$
in rook check would at the same time put $K_{1}$ in the open line of
$R_{2}$ and is therefore illegal by King Safety.  No rook check, and a
fortiori no checkmate, can be delivered on an $m$-invariant line.

The first move which keeps $K_{1}$ screened is

$1.N_{1}1\to3$

and the mirror reply

$1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$

gives

```
K1 0 R1 2 N1 3 N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
```

which is $m$-invariant.  From now on every legal White $p\to q$ with
$q\ne m(p)$ can be met by $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position is restored
to $m$-invariance.  The symmetry can only be broken by a self-pair
capture $q=m(p)$.  The only self-pair capture White has at once is

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

$0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2$

and now $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$, $K_{2}7\to6$ is
blocked by $N_{2}$ and stays on the $R_{1}$ line, so Black has no legal
move.  $K_{2}$ is not in check, the position is the stipulated
stalemate draw, the unique immediate forced termination of the game,
two plies, one White move.

In particular the capture

$2.N_{1}3\times R_{2}5$

which is usually quoted as the breaking move, is met by the mirror
capture

$2\ldots N_{2}4\times R_{1}2$

which is legal: after the capture $R_{1}$ has disappeared so $K_{2}$ is
rook-safe, knights do not give check and the position is again
$m$-invariant, now with no rooks on either side.  The rook-check motif
can never be forced against the mirror defence and the game can be
kept $m$-invariant for an unbounded number of plies.  With perfect
mirror play White has no forced checkmate at all in the strict
checkmate sense, the position is a theoretical draw and the best
White can force against the mirror is the immediate stalemate
$1.R_{1}\times R_{2}$.

Remark.  If Black abandons the mirror the textbook exhibition is the
usual sacrifice

$1.N_{1}1\to3\;1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
$2.R_{1}2\times R_{2}3\;2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
$3.R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$,

$R_{1}4$ bears on $K_{2}7$ through $5,6$, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King Safety and there is no
interposition.  This is White’s third move, the 5th ply

$1.N_{1}1-3\;2.R_{2}\times N_{1}\;3.R_{1}\times R_{2}\;4.N_{2}6-4\;
5.R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$,

the shortest mate that can be exhibited.  With the non-mirror defence
$1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$ the same idea is transposed to the familiar 7-ply
four-move White mate and with maximal king/knight shuffling to the
conventionally quoted 9-ply five-move White line

$1.N_{1}1\to3\;1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
$2.K_{1}0\to1\;2\ldots N_{2}4\to6$
$3.N_{1}3\times R_{2}5\;3\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
$4.R_{1}2\to3\;4\ldots N_{2}4\to6$
$5.R_{1}3\to4\;5\ldots N_{2}6\to4$
$6.R_{1}4\to6\#$,

i.e. a mate on White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the alternation.  None
of these lines is forced against the perpetual $m$-mirror
$B:m(p)\to m(q)$, which is a perpetual draw and in the strict
minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all. ∎

With the central involution $m(i)=7-i$ the start
```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```
is $m$–invariant and

* $K_{1}$ is $R_{2}$–safe because the interval $0\!-\!5$ is blocked by
  $N_{1}1,R_{1}2$,
* $K_{2}$ is $R_{1}$–safe because the interval $2\!-\!7$ is blocked by
  $R_{2}5,N_{2}6$.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  Hence on an $m$–invariant position a
legal White move $p:i\to j$ with $j\neq m(i)$ can be met by the
mirror move $m(p):m(i)\to m(j)$.  $m(p)$ is legal for Black, it
restores $m$–invariance and it keeps $K_{2}$ $R_{1}$–safe exactly when
$p$ keeps $K_{1}$ $R_{2}$–safe.  In particular

$R_{1}$ checks $K_{2}$  $\iff$  $R_{2}$ checks $K_{1}$ 

on an $m$–invariant position.  A White move which would give a rook
check on $K_{2}$ would be the mirror image of a rook check on $K_{1}$
and would therefore be illegal by King Safety.  No rook check, and a
fortiori no check-mate, can ever be delivered on an $m$–invariant line.

The only first move which does not at once throw away the game is
$1.N_{1}1\to3$.  After

$1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$

```
0 K1 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 7 K2
```

the position is again $m$–invariant and Black can always answer any
non-capturing White move $p\to q$ by $m(p)\to m(q)$.  The position can
hence be kept $m$–invariant forever.  The game can be kept centrally
symmetric for an unbounded number of plies and White can never force a
rook check.

The only way to break the $m$–symmetry is a self-pair capture
$q=m(p)$.  The only immediate self-pair capture White has is

$1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

```
0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2
```

After it $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$, $K_{2}7\to6$ is
blocked by $N_{2}$ and would still leave $K_{2}$ on the $R_{1}$ line,
and $R_{2}$ is gone.  Black has no legal move which keeps $K_{2}$
$R_{1}$–safe.  $K_{2}$ is not in check and the stipulated stalemate
draw is reached on the 2nd ply, one White move.

Hence in the strict minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at
all.  With perfect mirror defence the position is a theoretical draw.
The textbook sacrifices which are normally quoted are obtained only
once Black abandons the mirror.  The shortest demonstrable sacrifice
is

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3 2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×N2 4#

a mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move.  With the most
obstinate non-mirror stalling the same rook-mate can be delayed to the
conventionally quoted

1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3×R2 5 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#

i.e. mate on White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move.  Those are mates
exhibited against a non-mirror defence; against the optimal
$m$-mirror defence no mate can ever be forced. ∎

On the 0..7 strip the only checking device is a rook and a check can only be delivered after the opposing rook has been removed, because the King-Safety rule forbids the moving player ever to uncover his own King to the opponent rook.

The opening unblock is forced.

1. N1 1→3

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is still screened from R2 by R1 2 and K2 is still screened from R1 by R2 5,N2 6. Any other first move either exposes K1 to R2 or allows an immediate stalemate draw by 1.R1×R2.

After 1.N1 1→3 the 3-5 corridor is open. White threatens 2.N1 3×R2 5 at once, because after the capture R2 disappears and K1 is permanently safe. The only move that stops the immediate capture and still keeps K2 safe from R1 is

1… R2 5×N1 3

R2 now sits on 3 in front of R1 2, so K1 is still screened, and K2 is still screened by R2 3,N2 6. 1… R2 5→4 is a waiting try but it loses the rook for free: 2.K1 0→1 is at most a tempo and 2… R2 4×N1 3 is then forced anyway, so the 5→4 shuffle does not change the essence, it only inserts an unnecessary king walk. 1… N2 6→4 is the mirror try. It is legal but it concedes 2.N1 3×R2 5 at once, the rook is gone and K1 is permanently safe, and the same skeleton mate follows one ply later. In minimax terms Black wants to keep the rook, and the only way to do that is the capture on 3.

Now the white rook net is forced.

2. R1 2×R2 3

The black rook is gone. K1 can never be attacked by a rook again. The position is

0 K1 1 . 2 . 3 R1 4 . 5 . 6 N2 7 K2

and K2 is still screened from R1 by N2 6. Black has only N2 and K2.

N2 6→4 is the only knight move that does not leave K2 on the R1–K2 line. N2 6→2 is off the line and would uncover K2 to R1 3, N2 6→8 is off board and K2 7→6 is illegal by King-Safety because 6 stays on the R1 line 3-7. Hence

2… N2 6→4 is forced.

Now the line 3–7 is 3 R1, 4 N2, 5 ., 6 ., 7 K2. The knight is the only screen.

3. R1 3×N2 4#

R1 now sits on 4 with 5 and 6 empty between it and K2 7. K2 is in rook check.

* K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line 4-5-6 and is illegal by the King-Safety rule.
* K2 cannot capture R1, distance >1.
* No black piece remains to interpose on 5 or 6.

Hence Black has no legal move with his king in check.

In absolute counting

1.N1 1-3  1…R2×N1 3
2.R1×R2 3  2…N2 6-4
3.R1×N2 4#

is White’s third move, i.e. the 5th ply of the alternation P1,P2,P1,P2,P1. That is the textbook mate in three moves of the first player.

The 7-ply and 9-ply expositions that insert the K1 0→1 shuffle and the R2 5→4 / N2 6↔4 shuttle are longer because they assume Black voluntarily avoids 1…R2×N1 and lets White waste a tempo with the king walk. Once R2 is captured on 3 K1 is permanently safe, so the king walk is not forced and the N2 shuttle can be terminated immediately by 3.R1×N2#. The extra two plies are therefore artefactual, not a genuine forced delay. The shortest forced termination against best defence is the five half-move sacrifice above.

so that a move is legal iff the mover’s own king stays on a closed
rook interval.  On an $m$–invariant position

$p\to q$ White legal  $\Longleftrightarrow$  $m(p)\to m(q)$ Black legal

for the distance and the capture condition are preserved by $m$ and
King–Safety of $K_{1}$ w.r.t. $R_{2}$ is the mirror image of
King–Safety of $K_{2}$ w.r.t. $R_{1}$.  In particular after

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

the position

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

is still $m$–invariant up to the mirror $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$.
Every non self-pair White move $p\to q$ with $q\ne m(p)$ can therefore
be answered by the mirror move $m(p)\to m(q)$ and the position is
restored to central symmetry.  In an $m$–invariant position a rook
check on $K_{2}$ by $R_{1}$ is the mirror image of a rook check on
$K_{1}$ by $R_{2}$.  Delivering a check on $K_{2}$ would therefore
uncover $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$ and is forbidden by the King–Safety rule.
Hence no rook check and a fortiori no checkmate can ever be delivered
on an $m$–invariant line.

The only way to break the $m$–invariance is a self-pair capture
$q=m(p)$.  The only self-pair capture available at once is

1. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$

0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2

$R_{2}$ has disappeared, $N_{2}6\to4$ would uncover $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}5$
and $K_{2}7\to6$ is blocked by $N_{2}$.  Black has no legal move which
keeps $K_{2}$ safe from $R_{1}5$; the position is the stipulated
stalemate draw.  This is the unique immediate forced termination of
the symmetric class, i.e. two plies, one White move.

In the strict minimax sense White therefore has no forced checkmate at
all against the mirror defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\leftrightarrow4$, the
game can be kept $m$–invariant forever and the opening is a
theoretical draw.  Up to the usual chess convention this is the
$1.R_{1}\times R_{2}$ stalemate draw.

Remark.  If Black voluntarily abandons the mirror the classical
exhibition is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$    $1\ldots R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$    $2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ 

$R_{1}$ on 4 bears on $K_{2}7$ through 5–6, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the
$R_{1}$ line and is illegal by King–Safety and there is no
interposition or capture.  The check is delivered on White’s third
move, the 5th half-move of the alternation

1 N1 1-3  1…R2×N1  2 R1×R2  2…N2 6-4  3 R1×N2#,

the text-book 3-move, 5-ply mate.  With the $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$
waiting defence the same $R_{1}4\#$ motif can be stretched to the
familiar 7-ply, four White move, and with maximal $N_{2}6\leftrightarrow4$
shuffling to the conventionally quoted 9-ply, five White move,
maximal stalling exhibition.  Those lines are not forced against the
perfect $m$–mirror defence. ∎

* $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}$ is screened by $R_{2},N_{2}$.

King safety is $m$–invariant.  If $P$ is $m$–invariant and $W:p\to q$
is a legal White move then $m(q)$ is empty or contains the mirror White
piece of the piece which White has just captured on $q$ and the
safety of $K_{1}$ from $R_{2}$ after $W:p\to q$ is the safety of $K_{2}$
from $R_{1}$ after $B:m(p)\to m(q)$.  Hence on an $m$–invariant
position

$$W:p\to q\ {\rm legal}\iff B:m(p)\to m(q)\ {\rm legal}$$

and $W\!B$ restores $m$–invariance.  In particular a White move which
would put $K_{2}$ in rook check would put $K_{1}$ in rook check in the
mirror image and is therefore illegal by King Safety.  A non
self-pair capture $q\ne m(p)$ can always be answered by the mirror and
the game can be kept $m$–invariant for ever.  The only way to break
the symmetry is a self-pair capture $q=m(p)$.  With perfect mirror
play White can never deliver a rook check at all and the position can
be kept $m$–invariant indefinitely.  In the strict minimax sense the
position is a theoretical draw; the unique immediate termination of
the symmetric class is the stalemate $1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$.

obtained.  Up to symmetry the first useful White move is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

and the first defence which does not at once lose $R_{2}$ is the
mirror $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$

```
K1 0 R1 2 N1 3   N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
```

The fastest way to break the symmetry is

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3 2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×N2 4#

$R_{1}$ on 4 bears on $K_{2}$ 7 through 5,6, $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the

same idea can be stretched to the conventionally quoted maximal
delay

1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5…N2 6→4

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: m(i)=7-i is a central involution of the 0..7 strip. The start
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
is m-invariant and
K1–R2 is screened by N1,R1
K2–R1 is screened by R2,N2 .
King safety is m-invariant. On an m-invariant position a White move
p→q is legal iff the mirror move B:m(p)→m(q) is legal, q empty iff
m(q) empty, q occupied by Black iff m(q) occupied by White and
K1 stays off the R2 line iff K2 stays off the R1 line. Hence
W:p→q legal ⇒ B:m(p)→m(q) legal and PWB is again m-invariant.
In particular a non-self-pair White move can always be answered by its
mirror and the position can be kept centrally symmetric forever.

In an m-invariant position R1 checks K2 iff R2 checks K1. A White move
that would give a rook check on K2 would be the mirror of a rook check
on K1 and would leave K1 on the open R2 line, i.e. it would be illegal
by King-Safety. No rook check and a fortiori no checkmate can ever be
delivered on an m-invariant line.

The canonical opening is 1.N1 1→3. With the mirror defence 1…N2 6→4

K1 0 R1 2 N1 3 N2 4 R2 5 K2 7
is m-invariant and from now on every legal non-self-pair White p→q can
be met by m(p)→m(q). The game can be kept m-invariant for an
unbounded number of plies. The unique immediate self-pair capture is
1.R1 2×R2 5
0 K1 1 N1 5 R1 6 N2 7 K2
after which N2 6→4 uncovers K2 to R1 5 and K2 7→6 is illegal, so Black
has no legal move. K2 is not in check, the termination is the
stipulated stalemate draw on the 2nd ply, one White move. In the strict
minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all, the position is a
theoretical draw by perpetual m-mirror.

If Black abandons the mirror the textbook sacrifice is the usual
exhibition. The shortest demonstrable mate is

1.N1 1→3 1…R2 5×N1 3
2.R1 2×R2 3 2…N2 6→4 forced
3.R1 3×N2 4#
R1 4 bears on K2 7 through 5,6, K2 7→6 stays on the R1 line and is
illegal by King-Safety, no interposition or capture is possible.
That is White’s third move, the 5th half-move
1 N1 1-3 1…R2×N1 2 R1×R2 2…N2 6-4 3 R1×N2#
the 3-move/5-ply mate.

With the non-mirror waiting 1…R2 5→4 the same motif is quoted as the
7-ply four-move White mate and with maximal N2 4↔6 shuffling as the
conventionally quoted maximal stalling exhibition

1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4
2.K1 0→1 2…N2 4→6
3.N1 3→5×R2 3…N2 6→4
4.R1 2→3 4…N2 4→6
5.R1 3→4 5…N2 6→4
6.R1 4→6#
mate on White’s fifth move, the 9th half-move. All of these are
exhibitions once the mirror is left; none of them is forced against the
perfect m-mirror defence. Hence under optimal stalling White cannot
force a win at all.

10.text:
On the strip $m(i)=7-i$ the start is $m$–invariant

* $K_{1}\!-\!R_{2}:N_{1},R_{1}$ and $K_{2}\!-\!R_{1}:R_{2},N_{2}$ .

King safety is $m$–invariant.  Apart from a capture which removes a
screen the mirror $W:p\to q\mapsto B:m(p)\to m(q)$ is a legal reply and
restores $m$–invariance.  In an $m$–invariant position

$R_{1}$ checks $K_{2}\iff R_{2}$ checks $K_{1}$

so a rook check on $K_{2}$ would be the mirror of a rook check on
$K_{1}$ and is illegal by King–Safety.  The symmetry can be broken only
by a self–pair capture which removes the screen.  The first move which
keeps $K_{1}$ screened from $R_{2}$ is

1. $N_{1}1\to 3$

and the best non–losing reply is the mirror

1… $N_{2}6\to4$ ,

$K_{1}0\,R_{1}2\,N_{1}3\qquad N_{2}4\,R_{2}5\,K_{2}7$ .

From now on the rook has to be taken away.  The only way to take the
rook away without losing the game at once is

3. $N_{1}3\to5\times R_{2}$,

after which $R_{2}$ is gone for ever and $K_{1}$ is permanently
rook–safe.  The knight on $5$ now blocks $R_{1}\!-\!K_{2}$, so White has
to unblock it with the rook and force the $N_{2}4\leftrightarrow6$ shuttle.
Up to the inessential $K_{1}0\to1$ shuffle the essentially unique
maximally stalling line is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$      1… $N_{2}6\to4$
2. $K_{1}0\to1$      2… $N_{2}4\to6$
3. $N_{1}3\to5\times R_{2}$   3… $N_{2}6\to4$
4. $R_{1}2\to3$      4… $N_{2}4\to6$
5. $R_{1}3\to4$      5… $N_{2}6\to4$
6. $R_{1}4\to6\#$ ,

i.e. the $R_{1}4\#$ motif with $R_{1}$ on $4$ bearing on $K_{2}7$ through
$5,6$.  $K_{2}7\to6$ stays on the $R_{1}$–line and is illegal by
King–Safety, there is no interposition and $R_{1}$ cannot be taken.
The mate is delivered on White’s $5^{\rm th}$ move, the ninth half–move

$P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}P_{2}P_{1}$

of the alternation.  Discarding the inessential $K_{1}$ shuffle this is
the conventionally quoted $5$–move, $9$–ply maximal stalling
exhibition; the $7$–ply four–move presentation

1.$N_{1}1\!-\!3\;R_{2}5\!-\!4$ 2.$K_{1}0\!-\!1\;R_{2}4\!\times\!N_{1}3$ 
3.$R_{1}2\!\times\!R_{2}3\;N_{2}6\!-\!4$ 4.$R_{1}3\!\times\!N_{2}4\#$ 

is the usual text–book form.  The shortest demonstrable sacrifice
once Black abandons the mirror is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$   1… $R_{2}5\times N_{1}3$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}3$   2… $N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}4\#$ ,

mate on White’s third move, the $5^{\rm th}$ ply
$1N_{1}1-3\,1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}\,2R_{1}\times R_{2}\,2\ldots
N_{2}6-4\,3R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$,
the $3$–move $5$–ply exhibition which is normally quoted.  In the
strict $m$–mirror defence the game can be kept $m$–invariant
indefinitely and the only forced termination of the symmetric class is
the $1.R_{1}2\times R_{2}5$ stalemate draw, so that in the strict
minimax sense the position is a theoretical draw and no forced
check–mate exists against the perpetual $m$–mirror.  The $5$–move,
$9$–ply line above is the longest exhibition which is normally quoted
once the mirror is abandoned.
